verse: Then God said, “Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over the cattle and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
a: Man's creation came not by a word to the earth but by divine decree, proclaiming his distinction and pre-eminence above all creatures. The fathers saw the Trinity in the plural "Us," and "let them" includes male and female. Given dominion over every creature, man belongs to a sphere where God might display His eternal power and Godhead.
b: God created man in His image and likeness, giving him supreme authority over all living creatures. This likeness was not physical, but in man's moral and spiritual nature, originally marked by righteousness. Although sin has marred this divine image, through Christ, man can be transformed back into God's image. Man was to be the visible representative of God in the universe, the revelation side of His love and authority over creation, ultimately being transformed back into His likeness through Christ despite the effects of sin.

verse: but from the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You shall not eat from it or touch it, or you will die.’”
a: The woman, enchanted by unbelief, doubted God's warning about the tree in the garden, influenced by sensual desire and demonic spiritual interest. Deceived by the serpent's lies, she believed the false promise of enlightenment and divine knowledge through eating the forbidden fruit, leading to disobedience and humanity's fall. Influenced by the serpent's lies and desire, the woman believed the false promise of knowledge, leading to disobedience and humanity's fall.
b: The text presents man's normal destiny as eating of the tree of life, not of this tree of death. It appears God proved our first parents not through animal appetites but through their intellectual and moral nature. The death God warned of was separation from Him, shown when man, conscious he had no covering, was expelled from Eden.

verse: Also to Shem, the father of all the children of Eber, and the older brother of Japheth, children were born.
a: Shem is introduced with marked distinction as father of all the sons of Eber, from whom sprang the descendants of Abraham through Peleg and the Arabian tribe through Joktan. He is called Japheth's older brother, not Ham's. Shem's line stands in contrast to Nimrod's Babylon, the scene of man's glory and earthly imperial power.
b: Shem is specified as the father of all the sons of Eber, pointing to the Hebrew lineage of God's chosen people. The mention of him as the older brother of Japheth hints at their joint blessings and anticipated spiritual harmony, reflecting the eventual unity of Jewish and Gentile followers in the Christian church. Shem, father of Eber's lineage and elder brother to Japheth, hints at unity between Jewish and Gentile believers amidst Babylon's ongoing opposition to God's people.

verse: It came about when the sun had set, that it was very dark, and behold, there appeared a smoking oven and a flaming torch which passed between these pieces.
a: When the sun had set, Abram saw a smoking oven and a flaming torch. These symbols were manifestations of God, symbolizing His condescension to make a covenant with Abram and his descendants. The smoking furnace represented affliction, while the burning lamp signified God's light and salvation amidst darkness and trials. God uses the smoking furnace to signify affliction, but the burning lamp represents His light and salvation through trials, symbolizing the journey towards the inheritance amidst darkness and tests.
b: Jehovah manifested Himself to Abram in this symbol, as later in the pillar of cloud and fire. God alone passed between the pieces, ratifying the covenant. The smoke and flame showed that light would emerge out of darkness. The inheritance must be reached through the furnace, yet the darker its smoke, the brighter God's lamp of salvation.

verse: “This is My covenant, which you shall keep, between Me and you and your descendants after you: every male among you shall be circumcised.
a: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant, an institution of God and not of man. Abraham and his seed were to observe the rite. God promised Canaan for a perpetual possession. He also promised to be a God to his posterity. The rite was imperative, since there is no witness of God's people unless the flesh is set aside.
b: In establishing the covenant of circumcision with Abraham, God required every male, including those acquired as slaves, to undergo this sign of consecration and obedience. This directive, symbolizing sanctification and a covenant of blessing with Abraham's seed, emphasized the universal extension of God's promise to all nations. The act of circumcision was the initial step in a godly education, recognizing the obligation to fulfill further aspects of the covenant, extending its applicability beyond Abraham's immediate descendants to others as well. Through the act of circumcision, believers not only bear the covenant's seal but enter into a spiritual reality of death to flesh and new life in Christ, marking the beginning of a journey towards a life of consecration and obedience to God's covenant.

verse: now behold, this town is near enough to flee to, and it is small. Please, let me escape there (is it not small?) that my life may be saved.”
a: Instead of cheerfully obeying, Lot begged for refuge in the small and neighbouring city, Bela, afterwards called Zoar. He pleaded that it was a little one, perhaps meaning few inhabitants and few sins, or a small request not to be denied. Like a drowning man, he seemed to clutch at some little shred of the world rather than trusting God.
b: Lot, recognizing the angels as a manifestation of God, pleaded to flee to the small nearby city of Zoar to escape destruction. The visitors arranged Lot’s rescue, and with some urgency, the angels guided him to safety as the wicked townspeople demanded the men. Lot’s persistence was rewarded as he sought refuge in the little city, praying for his soul to be spared. Lot's plea, akin to a drowning man seeking hope, reflected a flawed desire for worldly security rather than complete trust in God's plan for his salvation.

verse: He spoke to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, saying, “If you will only please listen to me; I will give the price of the field, accept it from me that I may bury my dead there.”
a: Abraham, as a foreigner, approached the Hittites in a courteous manner to buy a burying-place, eventually offering to purchase the cave of Machpelah from Ephron. The negotiations for the land worth 400 shekels of silver were conducted publicly, with the money being uncoined silver, as seen when Abraham weighed it. Abraham approached the Hittites in faith, prepared to lay his head in the grave, understanding God's guidance as he purchased the cave of Machpelah for Sarah's burying-place.
b: Abraham addressed Ephron, owner of the field and apparently ruler of the city, before the people of the land. He asked as a favour to speak once more, declaring his determination to buy the land at its full worth for Sarah's burial. In paying the price, Abraham expressed his faith in resurrection, refusing to be debtor to those yet to be dispossessed.

verse: So Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and charged him, and said to him, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
a: Isaac was now alive to the real destiny of Jacob. He blessed him knowingly and willingly. He confirmed him as heir of the promise rather than revoking the blessing. His charge forbade marriage among the Canaanites, who were to be dispossessed of the land. Here commences Jacob's life of discipline, yet Isaac blessed where he might have rebuked, for God's purpose remained unaltered.
b: Isaac directed Jacob to avoid marrying Canaanites but to seek a wife among his mother's relatives in Padan-Aram. This act confirmed Jacob as the chosen heir of the promise and highlighted the significance of adhering to God's covenant, leading to both blessings and trials during his time away from home. Receiving divine blessings, Jacob is guided away from Canaanite wives by Isaac to fulfill God's covenant in Padan-Aram's providence amid his own weaknesses and God's sovereign grace.

verse: “Though you have felt through all my goods, what have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us two.
a: In the confrontation between Jacob and Laban, Jacob questions Laban about what he found after searching through his goods, highlighting the injustice and harsh treatment he endured despite serving Laban faithfully. Laban's corrupt practices and Rachel's cunning actions tainted their family dynamics, leading to a confrontation between Jacob's integrity and Laban's deceit. The tension escalates as Jacob asserts his innocence and readiness to settle the matter before their kin, confident that the truth will prevail in their judgment. "Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us two, commemorating a covenant of peace proposed, ratified by a sacrifice, and commemorated by a feast, reflecting the unseen hand of God settling the course of events."
b: When Laban found nothing, Jacob grew angry at the injustice of his hot pursuit and search among all his things. Was there any vessel or household item Laban could claim as his own? Acute sensibility gave Jacob's words a poetic form. Pursued as if a thief by his father-in-law, Jacob lays his complaint before their kinsmen to judge between them.

verse: Then they journeyed from Bethel; and when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth and she suffered severe labor.
a: Jacob's family left Bethel for Ephrath, where Rachel experienced intense labor pains while giving birth near Bethlehem. This unexpected event occurred only a short distance away, leading to the birth of Benjamin, meaning "the son of the right hand," representing strength and power. Throughout their journey, even in times of trial and loss, God remained present, providing guidance and strength to Jacob and his household. Rachel's sudden labor on the way to Ephrath near Bethlehem led to Benjamin's birth, symbolizing strength; revisiting the past at Bethel nurtured Jacob's faith and prepared him for future encounters with God.
b: Leaving Bethel after performing his vow, Jacob journeyed toward Ephrath with only a stretch of uncertain length remaining. On the way Rachel, whose wish for another son was about to be fulfilled, suffered the very birth-throes and anguish. Ephrath is Bethlehem, the House of Bread, and it is but a short distance from restored communion to nourishment.

verse: within three more days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office; and you will put Pharaoh’s cup into his hand according to your former custom when you were his cupbearer.
a: Joseph told the butler that in three days Pharaoh would restore him to his position, emphasizing that he was taken from his homeland unjustly. The dream's imagery explained the wine-making process, while divine intervention revealed the three-day time frame. The butler's restoration symbolized by lifting his head mirrored the baker's fate, indicating a return to his role as Pharaoh's cupbearer. His release by Pharaoh was symbolic of his return to his role as cupbearer, just as Joseph's exaltation led to humble service and divine wisdom, showcasing the fulfilling power of interpretations proclaimed.
b: The three branches meant three days, after which Pharaoh would restore him to his post. To lift up his head meant to raise him from his degradation and fetch him from prison. Squeezing grapes into Pharaoh's cup signified his restored service. Even in the prison God was working for Joseph, putting him in contact with the chief butler through this interpretation.

verse: As for the people, he removed them to the cities from one end of Egypt’s border to the other.
a: Joseph relocated the people of Egypt to cities throughout the land, not only for their convenience in accessing food stores but also to ensure they were not attached to the land as slaves. By distributing the population according to cities, avoiding the wasteful squandering of resources, and acknowledging Pharaoh's right to the land, Joseph implemented a strategic and compassionate approach to managing the famine. This relocation also served to prevent sedition and mutiny among the population, promoting a sense of unity and preventing potential unrest. Joseph's strategic relocation of Egypt's people across its borders, reminiscent of Christ's humility and God's sovereignty in disposing of royal inheritances and human hopes, reflected a compassionate and sovereign approach to managing the crisis.
b: Having secured the whole land to Pharaoh by purchase, Joseph removed the people to cities. This was evidently for the convenience of country people, who were doing nothing, to bring them where the corn stores were situated. In this exalted rule over Egypt's people, Joseph stands as a perfect and beautiful type of Christ in His glory.

verse: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them when he blessed them. He blessed them, every one with the blessing appropriate to him.
a: In Israel's twelve sons Jacob blessed the future tribes, his prophetic words referring not so much to the sons as to the tribes. Each received the blessing appointed of God, for Jacob pronounced what God had put into his mouth. These blessings looked forward to Christ, who sprang from Judah's tribe and is strikingly typified by Joseph.
b: Jacob's blessings over his twelve sons were not just personal affirmations but prophetic declarations of the future tribes of Israel. Receiving appropriate blessings, each tribe's unique destiny was foretold by Jacob, showing God's power to transform characters and impart blessings according to His plan. He blessed them, every one with the blessing appropriate to him, foretelling the future tribes of Israel, including the prophetic significance of Joseph and Judah as types of Christ, delineating the unique destinies of the twelve tribes.

verse: Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will surely take care of you and bring you up from this land to the land which He promised on oath to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.”
a: Facing death, Joseph gave the strongest proof of his faith and full assurance of the promises. The land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob meant Canaan, which God swore to give to their posterity. Though exalted in Egypt, Joseph was sure God would visit Israel, and his death was as lovely as his life.
b: Joseph, nearing death, assured his brothers of God's promise to bring them out of Egypt to Canaan, as He had sworn to their forefathers. This act of faith prompted Joseph to request his burial in Canaan, directing Israel's focus away from Egypt towards the land promised by God. Joseph, nearing death, emphasized God's pledge to bring his brothers to the promised land away from Egypt, aligning with the faith of the patriarchs in God's enduring promises.

verse: Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation.
a: After Joseph and all his brothers died, a significant increase in Israelites fulfilled God's promise and heightened the natural blessings of the land. This generation's passing marked the beginning of their trials, leading the descendants to remember their Canaanite roots and ensuring the fulfillment of God's ultimate plan. Joseph's death marked a significant transition for the Israelites, leading to trials that reinforced the need for simple trust in God's unfolding plan amidst the world's attempts to hinder His purpose.
b: The death of Joseph, his brethren and the whole family that first immigrated marks the beginning of a change. How long they survived their father is not said. Until then Israel, free from injustice and tyranny, peacefully enjoyed Egypt's hospitality. The story that left Joseph in a coffin would close with the glory of the Lord filling the tabernacle.

verse: When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the boy was crying. And she had pity on him and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
a: The exposure of the babe led the king's daughter to conclude he was a Hebrew child. His weeping most probably moved her compassion, and that feeling led her to save and adopt him in spite of her father's commands. The mother's faith had cleared the stage for God, who by His guiding care preserves what is precious in His sight.
b: The weeping Hebrew baby found by Pharaoh's daughter in the ark stirred her compassion, defying her father's decree as she chose to care for the child, unknowingly aligning with God's plan of salvation through her motherly instincts. Pharaoh's daughter, moved by the crying Hebrew child in the ark, defied her father's decree by showing compassion and caring for the baby, unwittingly playing a role in God's plan for the child's salvation as one of the Hebrews’ children.

verse: Then they came to Elim where there were twelve springs of water and seventy date palms, and they camped there beside the waters.
a: As the Israelites reached Elim, they found a place with twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, offering a much-needed rest stop on their journey. This oasis showcased God's provision in barren lands, with symbolic connections to the twelve tribes and seventy elders, demonstrating His care for His people in times of need. Elim symbolizes a place where God's satisfaction is found for those obedient and walking with Him, offering a taste of the heavenly Canaan for the Israelites journeying through the wilderness.
b: Elim, a lovely oasis in the barren desert, has been thought to bear the nation's stamp, a well for every tribe. Here Israel was to learn how the Lord could lead His people beside still waters, even in the barren desert of this life. Camped beside the waters, the redeemed found themselves surrounded by the fruits of God's salvation and His own grace.

verse: burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.
a: The verse illustrates the concept of retribution for harm inflicted, emphasizing the importance of fair compensation and protection within the community. It underscores the need for proper restitution for injuries by stipulating "burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise," ensuring exact reparation for the harm done. Requiring "burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise," the verse exemplifies the need for equitable reparation and safeguarding within society.
b: Burning flesh with fire fell under this rule of perfect retribution. So did wounds that let out blood. Stripes where the part turned black and blue fell under it too. Burns could not be literally repaid, so the rule guided the magistrate in awarding compensation. Such strict, even-handed justice shows God's amazing condescension to judge between man and man, and proves man's capability for violence.

verse: “Then you shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand and its base and its shaft are to be made of hammered work; its cups, its bulbs and its flowers shall be of one piece with it.
a: The candlestick was pure gold, beaten with a hammer from an entire mass, not poured into a mould. Its stem rested on a pedestal, and its flower cups, knobs and lilies were not made separately and joined. Set among God's priests, who need light as well as food, the golden lampstand points ahead to the glory of the Risen One.
b: The lampstand, made of pure gold in one piece, was intricately crafted with cups, bulbs, and flowers, symbolizing the Seven Spirits of God’s fullness. Positioned in the holy place, it signified the Church being illumined by Christ, the Light of the world, and the power of the Holy Spirit. This divine illumination was a vital element in the worship of God, emphasizing reliance on God's provision for the Church's guidance and preservation in darkness. The lampstand symbolizes the Church illumined by Christ and the Holy Spirit, emanating divine light founded on Christ's sacrifice empowered by the Spirit's energy.

verse: “You shall make fifty clasps of gold, and join the curtains to one another with the clasps so that the tabernacle will be a unit.
a: Fifty golden clasps were made to fasten the pieces of drapery, joining the curtains to create a unit for the tabernacle. These clasps united the two halves of the tent-cloth, enclosing the interior fully, including the walls and ceiling, with the gilded beams left uncovered inside. The clasps were crucial in joining the two halves of the curtains and forming the entire tabernacle-cloth to create a seamless dwelling place. The golden clasps signified Christ's perfect adjustment of God and man's claims, uniting the tabernacle as one consistent dwelling displaying His heavenly character reflected in the curtains and planks.
b: Fifty golden clasps fastened the two halves of the inner tent-cloth together, so that it might be one dwelling-place. This cloth formed the ceiling, and its joining came just above the curtain dividing the dwelling. In the couplings, the "clasps of gold" picture the unity of the saints in relation to all that is holy and blessed.

verse: “You shall take all the fat that covers the entrails and the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, and offer them up in smoke on the altar.
a: Amid the consecration of Aaron and his sons through anointing and sacrifices, the fat covering the entrails meant the thin membrane or skin in which the bowels are contained. This is the fold of membrane over the intestines, which generally bears much fat. Burned on the altar, these inward parts point to Christ, and God greatly delights in our true thoughts of Him.
b: During the consecration of the priests, specific parts of the animals were offered up as a sacrifice. It mentions taking "all the fat that covers the entrails" and burning it on the altar. The burning of the fat symbolizes offering the best to the Lord and signifies the need to subdue and restrain carnal desires and fleshly lusts. The need to subdue carnal desires and fleshly lusts is symbolized by the burning of the fat, emphasizing offering the best to the Lord through Christ's sin-offering character in priestly service.

verse: He joined five curtains to one another and the other five curtains he joined to one another.
a: This joining of curtains belongs to the preparation of the dwelling-place, the hangings and covering of the tabernacle, carried out just as God had earlier commanded. The work went forward with more than enough building material from the people's contributions. Such joined work may picture spiritual labour, by which the saints are drawn together in their appreciation of Christ.
b: Skilled workmen executed the construction of the tabernacle according to previous instructions. The curtains were joined in groups of five, as specified, by craftsmen skilled in various materials like metal, stone, and wood, using wool and linen for the cloths. They followed every instruction precisely to take character from Christ and relate to one another divinely, leading to Jehovah's glorious presence filling the completed tabernacle.

verse: and a bulb was under the first pair of branches coming out of it, and a bulb under the second pair of branches coming out of it, and a bulb under the third pair of branches coming out of it, for the six branches coming out of the lampstand.
a: The lampstand in the tabernacle displayed bulbs under each pair of branches, totaling six altogether. This detailed design was a key part of preparing the sacred vessels, such as the ark of the covenant, the table of showbread, the candlestick, the altar of incense, the anointing oil and incense, the altar of burnt-offering, the laver, and the court. The craftsmanship of each element symbolized the holiness of the entire sanctuary. A missing peg would mean a slack cord, and a slack cord would mean a curtain out of place, and so the disorder would spread, reminding us of the essential details in manifesting God's glory through the tabernacle's intricate design.
b: The candlestick's bulbs set beneath each pair of its six branches belong to the vessels of the dwelling, made as directed before. Such minute listing shows a careful and exact obedience, everything done according to Jehovah's commandment. Each bulb is part of Christ's glory, and letting one detail drop out loses a ray of that glory.

verse: He overlaid it with pure gold, its top and its sides all around, and its horns; and he made a gold molding for it all around.
a: The altar of incense was among the vessels of the dwelling. It was overlaid with pure gold on top, sides and horns. It was also given a gold molding. Such work was careful and exact obedience to Jehovah's commandment, showing the Old covenant again established. Made according to the divine pattern, without man's expediency, the tabernacle could therefore be filled with the divine glory.
b: Crafted by Bezaleel, the construction of the sanctuary involved several sacred objects, such as the ark of the covenant, the table of shew-bread, the candlestick, the altar of incense, the anointing oil, the altar of burnt-offering, the laver, and the court. The ark, the most holy item, was crafted by Bezaleel. The use of gold and silver in the various items highlighted the value and significance of these vessels. Overlaying the ark with pure gold inside and out, including its horns, reflected the divine pattern meticulously followed in every detail, emphasizing the sanctuary's readiness to be filled with God's glory.

verse: He made two golden rings for it under its molding, on its two sides—on opposite sides—as holders for poles with which to carry it.
a: Crafting sacred vessels for the dwelling involved detailed preparation, with each item serving a specific function and holding significance. The construction order, like the creation of the ark of the covenant, table of shew-bread, candlestick, and others, emphasized the importance of these items within the sanctuary. The intricacies of overlaying certain parts with gold or silver, enumerating the materials used, and the careful design of each utensil reflected the meticulous care taken in carrying out God's instructions for the sacred space. Crafting each detail faithfully in accordance with God's instructions reflected the true devotion of the people, where their hearts were stirred to wholehearted obedience without room for man's reason, simply doing as they were told.
b: The golden rings belonged to the altar of incense, made just as Jehovah had earlier directed. This work reflects the people's enthusiasm and joy joined with a careful, exact obedience to the law, doing everything according to Jehovah's commandment. Every pin and ring followed the divine pattern, leaving no room for man's expediency, so the tabernacle could be filled with divine glory.

verse: The skillfully woven band which was on it was like its workmanship, of the same material: of gold and of blue and purple and scarlet material, and fine twisted linen, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
a: The woven band belonged to the ephod, the shoulder-dress that formed the principal part of the high priest's official robes. Its making in gold, blue, purple and scarlet was an exact obedience to the law, rendered primarily to Moses. Conformity to the divine pattern left no room for man's expediency, so the tabernacle could be filled with divine glory.
b: The clothing of the priests, such as the ephod, breastplate, over-coat, body-coats, turbans, drawers, and girdles, were meticulously made with materials of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen as God commanded Moses. The order of the garments, from the ephod to the diadem on Aaron's turban, displayed the importance and honor of the priests. The detailed workmanship and symbolism of each garment highlighted the sacredness and reverence of their role in serving God. The priests' devotion was evident in the meticulous details and materials like gold, blue, purple, and scarlet, showing their obedience to God's pattern.

verse: He placed the laver between the tent of meeting and the altar and put water in it for washing.
a: The laver stood between the dwelling and the altar, probably placed more to the side, so the priests need not go round the altar. Its water, for washing hands and feet, held the means of purification for the sacrificial service. Moses alone set it in place, all according to the divine pattern, leaving no room for man's expediency.
b: The laver was strategically placed between the tent of meeting and the altar, possibly off to the side, ensuring the priests did not need to circle around the altar for washing. This positioning allowed them to purify themselves before approaching the sacred spaces, reflecting a deeper spiritual cleansing offered in the future through a laver or fountain like in Zechariah 13:1. Reflecting a deeper spiritual cleansing, the laver positioned by the tent of meeting allowed priests to purify themselves before approaching sacred spaces, mirroring a future cleansing fountain as seen in Zechariah 13:1.

verse: ‘Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy.
a: The verse states that “Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy.” The flesh of the sin-offering was to be eaten only by male priests after boiling, distinguishing between sin-offerings for the laity and high priest/congregation. This act signifies a sacred and consecrated practice for the priests. Feeding on Christ, the priest must understand how the offering serves God, nourishing the holy priesthood and receiving the portion devoted to God before indulging in this sacred act.
b: The flesh of the sin-offering was eaten by the males among the priests alone. This meant not only the offering priest but his male children and other priests upon duty. It applied only to sin-offerings of the laity. Called "most holy," it nourished the priest inwardly upon the holy grace in which Christ bore sin's judgment.

verse: but what is left over from the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned with fire.
a: Whatever flesh remained uneaten after the second day was to be destroyed by burning on the third. This was commanded not to compel the person bringing the offering to invite the poor, but to guard against desecration of the meal. Such limits guarded the enjoyment of spiritual good in communion, preparing saints to partake intelligently of the Lord's table.
b: The leftover flesh of the sacrifice on the third day is to be burned with fire to prevent it from becoming putrid and desecrating what is holy. Eating it on the third day is considered an abomination, leading to bearing sin, showing the importance of following God's instructions precisely to avoid defiling the sacrifice. The remains of the sacrifice left on the third day must be burned to prevent defilement, pointing to the significance of following God's instructions precisely, especially in communion and priestly service, which result in personal gain and spiritual nourishment through Christ.

verse: Then he slaughtered the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings which was for the people; and Aaron’s sons handed the blood to him and he sprinkled it around on the altar.
a: After consecrating the sin and burnt offerings, Aaron proceeded with the peace offering for the congregation, signifying communion with God and rejoicing in accepted sacrifices. The blood was sprinkled around the altar to show atonement and acceptance by the Almighty, with Aaron's sons assisting in the presentation to ensure the offering's proper execution. By participating in presenting the offering and assisting in its execution, Aaron's sons actively demonstrated the significance of Christ's sacrifice in ensuring communion and rejoicing in acceptance by the Almighty.
b: The peace-offering came last in Aaron's appointed order, after the sin-offering and burnt-offering. It showed forth the communion granted to those justified and sanctified. The people might feast and rejoice that atonement was made for their sins. The sprinkled blood points to Christ, who as sacrifice introduces His people into a settled relationship with God.

verse: ‘Also whoever touches the person with the discharge shall wash his clothes and bathe in water and be unclean until evening.
a: Whoever touched the flesh, that is, the body, of the man with the discharge was defiled. Such a one was unclean in consequence and had to bathe himself and wash his clothes, remaining unclean until evening. Even seemingly unavoidable weaknesses defiled and required cleansing, because Jehovah was in the camp.
b: Touching someone with a discharge makes a person unclean; they must wash their clothes, bathe, and remain unclean until evening. Anyone who touches the affected person, their belongings, or sits on their bed becomes unclean too. This indicates a call for both moral and physical purity among the Israelites. Whoever touches the individual with a discharge must wash and bathe, symbolizing the necessity for moral cleansing to partake in holy privileges related to God's tabernacle, emphasizing the significance of purification through God's word.

verse: ‘Likewise, whoever touches them shall be unclean and shall wash his clothes and bathe in water and be unclean until evening.
a: Whoever touched those things, her bed and seat, defiled by a woman's diseased issue flowing beyond her monthly impurity, was himself unclean. He must wash his clothes and bathe, dipping the body all over, remaining unclean until the even. Such cleansing was required because Jehovah was in the camp, and nothing unfitting could be suffered within His sacred precincts.
b: A woman with a prolonged or irregular issue of blood was considered unclean, making anyone who touched her or her belongings unclean as well until evening. This law, extending the uncleanness beyond the normal monthly period, served as a deterrent to immoral behavior. Even in her uncleanness, the woman was still allowed to carry out her daily tasks. Whoever touches the unclean shall wash, illustrating a moral purification through God's word, which brings Christ's love to bear upon us, setting aside uncleanness to approach God's presence with purity.

verse: “The goat shall bear on itself all their iniquities to a solitary land; and he shall release the goat in the wilderness.
a: The living goat, laden with the confessed sins, was quite as truly a sin-offering as the slaughtered one. It was led into the desert, not to find its way back. This symbolized complete deliverance from sin and its author. Both goats looked onward to but one comprehensive sacrificial act, the atonement of Christ, which alone could fully glorify God.
b: The goat, signifying the bearer of sins and a sin-offering, symbolizes Israel's deliverance from sin and its author, Azazel. By carrying sins into the wilderness, the goat completes the removal of confessed sins, like Christ bearing the sins of His people on the cross. The release of the goat signifies the freedom from sin granted to Israel. Into a land not inhabited, the goat bears the sins, completing their removal to a solitary place, like Christ removing sins on the cross, signifying Israel's deliverance.

verse: ‘Do not profane your daughter by making her a harlot, so that the land will not fall to harlotry and the land become full of lewdness.
a: The command forbids physical prostitution, not spiritual idolatry, and the word for lewdness, zimmah, belongs to that connection. Rather than restricting the law to public stews, God commands parents to preserve their daughters through a pure and chaste education. Such impurity shows man as corrupted by Satan and corrupting himself, the old man bearing no feature of God.
b: Parents are warned not to allow their daughters to be involved in prostitution, as this would lead to widespread immorality in the land. This prohibition is specific to physical whoredom, not spiritual idolatry, emphasizing the importance of preserving purity and chastity in society through proper upbringing and education. May we never allow a tale to pass our lips, ensuring reverence for those who preserve purity as a precious reflection of God's holiness in relationships, guiding us to honor each accordingly and uphold parental influence.

verse: nor shall he approach any dead person, nor defile himself even for his father or his mother;
a: The high priest, anointed with oil, was to maintain a spotless purity in a higher degree still. He might not enter a tent or house where a dead body lay, nor defile himself even for father or mother. Nearness to God demanded holiness, so even sorrow for the nearest dead had to be controlled by his priestly calling.
b: The high priest, consecrated with anointing oil and sanctified to wear holy garments, was forbidden from defiling himself by coming into contact with the dead, even his own parents. This extreme purity extended to mourning customs, funerals, and leaving the sanctuary, ensuring no defilement of his consecration. Nor shall he defile himself, even for his father or his mother, as a priest's natural feelings should be under restraint to maintain holiness before God.

verse: “On exactly the tenth day of this seventh month is the day of atonement; it shall be a holy convocation for you, and you shall humble your souls and present an offering by fire to the LORD.
a: This unusual festival on the tenth day of the seventh month expiated the sins of the whole year. In holy convocation the people afflicted their souls by repentance, contrition and fasting, and offered a burnt offering to the LORD. An awakened, revived people afflict their souls, a humbling exercise leading to great appreciation of Christ's death and the Mercy-seat.
b: The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement, a time of solemn observance that requires fasting, resting from work under penalty of death, and presenting offerings to the Lord. During this day, repentance and contrition for sins are emphasized, as well as seeking forgiveness through atonement and acknowledging guilt before God. The severity of the penalty for transgressions against the day's requirements highlights the importance of sincere repentance and reconciliation with God through His gracious forgiveness. Humbling themselves and abstaining from work, the people of God partake in the holy convocation of the Day of Atonement, presenting fire offerings to the Lord to find perfect peace and acknowledge their need for His gracious forgiveness.

verse: “Then you shall take fine flour and bake twelve cakes with it; two-tenths of an ephah shall be in each cake.
a: Twelve unleavened cakes made with two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour each were placed on the golden table in the tabernacle as an offering and memorial before Jehovah. This "bread of faces" represented the twelve tribes of Israel, signifying an everlasting covenant and God's favor towards His people. The meticulous preparation and placement of the loaves underscored the holiness of the offering and the unity of the nation in their relationship with God. The twelve loaves on the golden table portrayed Israel's unity before God, symbolizing the everlasting covenant with each cake representing Christ in connection with the tribes and flagging faith's certainty in God's constant care.
b: The twelve cakes of fine flour, answerable to the twelve tribes, were baked by Levites from flour furnished by the people. Each held two-tenths of an ephah, and since they entered the sanctuary before Jehovah, they were almost certainly unleavened. Speaking of the saints as having Christ as their life, the twelve cakes stood before God as "a bread of remembrance".

verse: ‘He shall then go out from you, he and his sons with him, and shall go back to his family, that he may return to the property of his forefathers.
a: A person who became a servant due to debts or poverty in ancient Israel was granted release, along with their family, to return to their ancestral property during the year of Jubilee. This release signifies the principle of God's redemption and the abolishment of slavery within the theocracy. All Israel shall be saved, and God's unfailing grace will assert itself as the trumpet of jubilee sounds, allowing each to return to their possession, blotted out by the day of atonement.
b: The Israelite who sold himself from poverty was kept not as a slave. He was kept as a day-labourer and temporary resident. He went free in the Jubilee with his sons. He returned to his father's family and to the allotment Jehovah had given them. Jehovah can never give up that land, and in sovereign mercy the jubilee trumpet returns every one to his possession.

verse: ‘I shall also grant peace in the land, so that you may lie down with no one making you tremble. I shall also eliminate harmful beasts from the land, and no sword will pass through your land.
a: The Lord promised peace in the land, suffering no war to come over it. He would cause beasts of prey that endanger life, such as lions, bears and wolves, to vanish out of the land of Israel. Such peace rested on Israel's obedience, for the arm of Jehovah could never be stretched forth to shield unholy living or disobedience.
b: God promises peace in the land of Israel, where the people can rest without fear, as wild animals are removed and enemies kept at bay. The Lord will ensure the safety of His people, granting them freedom from internal conflict and external threats, ultimately fulfilling His covenant with them. Obedience to God ensures peace and security for Israel, shielding them from harm and conflict, allowing them to rest in His favor despite potential adversities.

verse: ‘He shall not replace it or exchange it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good; or if he does exchange animal for animal, then both it and its substitute shall become holy.
a: When someone devoted an animal to the Lord as a vow, it had to remain as is without being exchanged for a better or worse one. This precaution ensured the sanctity of the vow and discouraged any deceptive behavior or attempts to improve upon what was dedicated to God. Each hallowed gift signifies a surrendered heart to the Lord that cannot be exchanged, as all devotedness is prized by God and reflects a profound sense of value.
b: A beast vowed to Jehovah was holy and not to be exchanged, good for bad or bad for good. Should such an exchange be made, both the animal first dedicated and its substitute became holy, not to be redeemed. Devoted things stand by the Lord's own valuation, for He takes account of them and makes no mistakes.

verse: of Zebulun, Eliab the son of Helon;
a: Eliab the son of Helon stood as head of the tribe of Zebulun, one of the leaders named over the fathers' houses into which each tribe was arranged. Such men were no doubt counted renowned among their fellows. Under such heads, hardly could an Israelite numbered for warfare be unable to declare his pedigree or recognize his standard.
b: Moses and Aaron were instructed to count the people with the help of a leader from each tribe who represented the mishpachoth or families of the tribes. These heads of tribes were known as "called men of the congregation" and "princes of the tribes of their fathers." The names of the leaders, such as Eliab the son of Helon from Zebulun, were carefully selected and held in high esteem among their people. Eliab the son of Helon from Zebulun was carefully chosen to represent his mishpachah, showing the importance of knowing one's spiritual lineage for battle in God's army.

verse: of Gad, Eliasaph the son of Deuel;
a: Eliasaph the son of Deuel stood as Gad's tribe-prince, chosen to help Moses and Aaron muster the people. Such princes were heads of the thousands of Israel, and their names attest the religious mind of the people. Gad's numbering views the assembly in its competency for war, counting only the full grown who quit themselves like men.
b: The verse mentions the tribe of Gad, represented by Eliasaph the son of Deuel, one of the leaders assisting Moses and Aaron in mustering the people. These captains were designated as “princes of the tribes of their fathers” and “heads of the thousands of Israel,” each representing their tribe and assisting in managing national affairs. Every leader like Eliasaph the son of Deuel had a specific post and pedigree, essential for order in the congregation's walk and warfare, highlighting divine assignments and individual qualifications.

verse: These are the names of the sons of Gershon by their families: Libni and Shimei;
a: The sons of Gershon, Libni and Shimei, were part of the Levites sanctified to Jehovah as replacements for the first-born. Gershon's descendants, through Libni and Shimei, formed the Libnite and Shimite families, integral parts of the Levite tribe assisting in the Tabernacle duties. Each Levite's distinct service in the tabernacle, be it carrying pegs or candlesticks, worked harmoniously towards the common goal of maintaining divine order and fulfilling their unique responsibilities.
b: Gershon, son of Levi, had two sons, Libni, meaning white, and Shimei, meaning Jah is prince of praise. These were founders of the clans among the Levites, two families called after their names and now numbered. Their descendants camped behind the tabernacle westward and carried its curtains, coverings, cords, hangings, and woven and embroidered work.

verse: one gold pan of ten shekels, full of incense;
a: The princes of the tribes each presented the same gifts, with the tribe of Judah leading and Naphtali ending the procession. The offerings, including a gold pan filled with incense, were repeated twelve times, one for each tribe, symbolizing the equal honor placed on each tribe and their part in protecting God's treasures. These offerings, though the same, were given with care and attention, reminding us that God remembers and values even the smallest acts of love and devotion. God appreciates every act, however small, given with care, symbolizing equal honor on each tribe, showcasing the cheerful and valued service to God by all.
b: The golden spoon, or pan, weighed ten shekels and was full of incense, though the word shekel is invariably omitted in the weights. Belonging to the dedication of the altar, the twelve offerings were strictly alike, given on separate days. Not without significance, the gold cup weighs only ten shekels, its incense perhaps answering to Paul's prayers in Ephesians.

verse: ‘The LORD is slow to anger and abundant in lovingkindness, forgiving iniquity and transgression; but He will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and the fourth generations.’
a: Describing the LORD as forgiving towards all sins, the passage highlights His abundant mercy and justice in visiting past iniquities. Moses pleads for mercy for the Israelites, emphasizing God's oath and His revelation of character. This demonstrates the importance of understanding God's longsuffering and grace in dealing with His people. God's mercy and justice are displayed as Moses intercedes for the Israelites, emphasizing God's longsuffering and unwillingness to clear the guilty, while the consequences of unbelief are evident in the harsh reality faced by the murmuring generation.
b: Moses brings forward the word in which God Himself had revealed His deepest being at Sinai, appealing to the consistency of divine grace. His plea was not that the guilty be cleared altogether, but that God show mercy rather than cut off the whole nation. Yet government stands beside grace: Israel was pardoned, but that generation fell, God's hand making good what His mouth uttered.

verse: Then Moses arose and went to Dathan and Abiram, with the elders of Israel following him,
a: Moses, following Jehovah's instruction, directed the congregation to stay away from the tents of the rebellious men, Dathan and Abiram, to prevent being affected by their sins. The elders of Israel accompanied Moses to support him in confronting the factions and upholding God's law through divine judgment. Moses, accompanied by the elders of Israel as a shield, approached Dathan and Abiram in a moment of divine judgment amid rebellion, demonstrating the importance of intercession by Moses and Aaron to prevent disaster.
b: Moses went to the tents of Dathan and Abiram, the Reubenite faction who had refused obedience with malignant irony. With the elders following, he sought to convince them of their evil and reclaim them from their folly. Their quarrel was with God, not Moses, and they might have found salvation recognizing the place God gave him.

verse: These are the families of the sons of Gad according to those who were numbered of them, 40,500.
a: The Gadites, numbering 40,500, match the list of Gad's sons in Genesis, except that Ozni is there called Ezbon. Differences in names may arise because grandsons appear as sons, or because some had probably died childless without founding distinct families. Such numbering governed the land's division, where "to the many thou shalt increase their inheritance," yet all fell by lot.
b: The families of the sons of Gad, numbered at 40,500, are descendants of the Gadites mentioned in Genesis 46:16, although Ezbon is identified as Ozni. The sons of Korah, descendants of those spared from Korah's judgment, were granted a remarkable deliverance from destruction, illustrating the profound grace of God throughout history.

verse: These are the families of Levi: the family of the Libnites, the family of the Hebronites, the family of the Mahlites, the family of the Mushites, the family of the Korahites. Kohath became the father of Amram.
a: The verse in question identifies the families of Levi, including the Libnites, Hebronites, Mahlites, Mushites, and Korahites. This enumeration serves to trace back the lineage of prominent figures like Moses and Aaron to their ancestor Levi through Kohath, concluding with a total of 23,000 Levites counted in the census. Kohath became the father of Amram, showcasing the lineage that traces notable figures such as Moses and Aaron back to their ancestor Levi through the Libnites, Hebronites, Mahlites, Mushites, and Korahites, with particular grace shown to the sons of Korah despite their undeserving nature.
b: The census of Levi was taken separately, on a different principle from the rest. Among its families, the Hebronites traced to Kohath, the Mahlites and Mushites to Merari, and the Korahites to Korah. Moses and Aaron were descendants of Kohath. Wonderful to say, the sons of Korah, least deserving as man would think, were exempted by God's special grace.

verse: But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered strange fire before the LORD.
a: Nadab and Abihu were sons of Aaron, named within the counting of the Levites. Though the Levites, having no inheritance, occupy little space in this outline, the sons of Aaron come into great prominence. Their death for offering "strange fire before the LORD" is recorded even in a family numbering viewing the inheritance.
b: Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, died for offering strange fire before the Lord. The Levites are listed, with three chief houses and Aaron's descendants. The text underscores the ancestral lineage and the significant number of Levites. Their lack of faith led Nadab and Abihu to offer strange fire before the LORD, resulting in their demise; faith, vital for liberation and salvation, sets apart God's people and precedes the Levites' lineage.

verse: “The rest of Gilead and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh, all the region of Argob (concerning all Bashan, it is called the land of Rephaim.
a: In the distribution of the conquered land, Moses apportioned the southern portion to the Reubenites and Gadites and the northern half of Gilead and all of Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh. Bashan was known as a land of giants, labeled the land of Rephaim for its association with these formidable inhabitants. God gave the land of Bashan, known for its giants, to the half-tribe of Manasseh, just as He empowered the Israelites to conquer Og, the formidable king of Bashan, as a result of their obedience to Him.
b: Moses reviews the distribution of the conquered land. He recalls giving the rest of Gilead and all Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh. Bashan was the kingdom of Og. The region of Argob, Trachonitis in Bashan, passed for a land of giants. East of Jordan, not in Canaan, they indicate territory to be taken from the flesh's power and held for God.

verse: He brought us out from there in order to bring us in, to give us the land which He had sworn to our fathers.’
a: The Lord brought Israel out of a state of bondage and misery by means of miraculous plagues, so that He might bring them into Canaan. He would give them possession of it, fulfilling His oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The land was ever God's objective, a free gift where every city, well and vine spoke of His infallible faithfulness.
b: God delivered the Israelites from Egypt to bring them into the promised land, as He had sworn to their forefathers. By instructing their children about God's commandments and miraculous deeds, the Israelites aimed to instill a reverence for the Lord in the younger generation, emphasizing the importance of faith and righteousness in following His ways and avoiding idolatry. The commandment to swear by His Name highlights the exclusivity of devotion to the God of Israel and the seriousness of invoking His Name in oaths. The commandment to swear by His Name underscores the dedication to the God of Israel and the solemnity of invoking His Name in oaths, reflecting His infallible faithfulness in bringing His people to the promised land.

verse: “You shall remember all the way which the LORD your God has led you in the wilderness these forty years, that He might humble you, testing you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep His commandments or not.
a: Israelites were led through the wilderness for forty years for a purpose: to humble them, test their obedience, and reveal what was truly in their hearts. Their journey was full of both hardships and blessings, meant to show them their need for God's help and to prove their faithfulness to His commandments. The provision of manna was a miraculous reminder that obedience to God is more important than anything else, even sustenance. Through their trials and blessings, God was both disciplining and blessing His people, leading them to a deeper understanding of His ways and their own hearts. God's purpose in leading the Israelites through the wilderness for forty years was to humble them and test their obedience, demonstrating their dependence on Him above all, as seen in the provision of manna and other trials, revealing their true faithfulness to His commandments.
b: Israel was to remember the forty years' guidance through the wilderness, by which God desired to humble them. Through temptations and humiliations He sought to train them to obedience, and to prove the state of their heart and their obedience. The wilderness tested submission to God, showing that what He can be there is as important as the land's wealth.

verse: that his heart may not be lifted up above his countrymen and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, to the right or the left, so that he and his sons may continue long in his kingdom in the midst of Israel.
a: The Israelite king was instructed to keep a copy of the law by his side and read it daily in order to stay humble, avoid pride, and remain obedient to God's commandments throughout his reign. By following these guidelines, the king and his descendants would rule long and prosper in their hereditary kingdom, ensuring the continuity of leadership within the family as long as they walked in God's ways. To prevent pride and deviation from God's ways, the king must keep the law close, ensuring long reign and prosperity within his hereditary kingdom amidst Israel.
b: Keeping the law by him, the king was not to deviate in the least from God's law in his kingly office. From this it appears the crown in Israel was to be hereditary, unless forfeited by personal crime. God would delight that one truly a brother, whose heart is lowly, should hold a place of influence among His people.

verse: “For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD; and because of these detestable things the LORD your God will drive them out before you.
a: Those who practice detestable acts are abominable to the Lord, leading to their removal from His presence. This abomination was the reason for the expulsion of the Canaanites before Israel, showcasing the severe consequences of indulging in such sinful practices. The importance of seeking divine guidance and following God's laws is highlighted to avoid facing a similar fate. For all who engage in these abominable practices are detestable to the Lord, leading to their expulsion, emphasizing the importance of abiding by God's laws to avoid a similar fate.
b: Whoever practised pagan omen-reading, fortune-telling and witchcraft was an abomination to the Lord. Because of this abomination He rooted out the Canaanites before Israel. This striking example deters Israel from imitating sins so severely punished. The true believer rejects such things as worthless rubbish, resting in holy tranquility in God's peerless Revelation graciously given.

verse: “But if there is a man who hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and rises up against him and strikes him so that he dies, and he flees to one of these cities,
a: The cities of refuge were not meant as places of safety for criminals deserving of death, nor to shelter one who had slain a neighbour out of hatred. Such a man lay in wait and struck him mortally, so that he died. The land Jehovah gave must have justice, and loving-kindness or pleasant affections must not turn aside the sentence of righteousness.
b: If a man harbors hatred and premeditates to kill his neighbor, striking him so that he dies, he is to seek refuge in the designated cities. Witnesses were crucial, ensuring a thorough inquiry and emphasizing the sanctity of human life through the law of "life for life." In detailing the establishment of these cities, the passage highlights the significance of preparing specific roads for the fugitives, symbolizing justice and protection. Finding refuge in the cities was crucial for the man who harbored hatred and intentionally killed, as God's provision ensured his safety within the designated areas, offering a sanctuary symbolizing divine grace and justice.

verse: “When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, so that you will not bring bloodguilt on your house if anyone falls from it.
a: When constructing a new house, it is essential to add a balustrade to the roof to avoid endangering lives. The flat roofs of ancient houses were used for various activities, making the addition of a protective railing a wise precaution. Not only does this practice promote safety and prevent accidents, but it also reflects a spirit of humanity and care for others, as failing to provide this safety measure could lead to disastrous consequences. In building a new house, ensuring a parapet for the roof showcases a spirit of consideration for others' safety in daily activities, illustrating the meticulous care God extends even to the smallest details of His people's lives.
b: Israelite roofs were flat and often lived upon, so a parapet or railing was almost a necessary protection. Without it, carelessness could expose human life to danger and defile the house with blood if anyone fell from it. The Lord would have His people thoughtful of others' safety, not merely their own convenience, building with care against every point of danger.

verse: “Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt.
a: Remember the incident with Miriam, how she was afflicted with leprosy for rebelling against Moses after coming out of Egypt. This serves as a warning against speaking evil of those in authority or entertaining suspicions, emphasizing the consequences of such actions through the example of Miriam being shut up for seven days because of her rebellion. Afflicted with leprosy, Miriam's rebellion stands as a warning against speaking ill of authority, underlining the consequences through her seven-day isolation as a result of her actions.
b: Miriam brought leprosy upon herself as a punishment for her rebellion against Moses. Yet what Jehovah did to her is in view. This was her separation beyond the camp. It warns Israel to watch diligently lest they incur the plague of leprosy. Yet God disowns what stood related to Him only after much long-suffering, lingering in the reluctance of love.

verse: “For everyone who does these things, everyone who acts unjustly is an abomination to the LORD your God.
a: Moses emphasizes the duty of integrity in trade, summing up all breaches of the law as abominations to the Lord who hates injustice. This verse serves as a reminder of God's righteous character in human behavior. For everyone who does these things, everyone who acts unjustly is an abomination to the Lord your God, reflecting God's righteous character in human behavior by condemning all breaches of the law as abominations.
b: The duty of integrity in trade is enforced once more. With the words "all that do unrighteously," Moses sums up all breaches of the law, whatever is not just and right between man and man, as abomination before the LORD. The Lord pays back anything ungracious in our spirits or ways, for those who do wrong receive the wrong they have done.

verse: and He has brought us to this place and has given us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.
a: God's faithfulness to His people is seen from the beginning when He delivered Jacob and his family to Egypt, which led to their multiplication into a great nation. The act of bringing the Israelites from Egypt to the promised land of abundance was a fulfilled promise that evoked gratitude. The land of Canaan, flowing with milk and honey, was a tangible reminder of God's provision and goodness throughout their journey. He came down to bring the Israelites to the land flowing with milk and honey, where their worship and praise culminated in giving back to God what was rightfully His.
b: The one bringing the first-fruits confesses that God has brought Israel into this land, the land of Canaan. Its usual description as flowing with milk and honey speaks of its great fertility and the abundance of good things in it. It is good to retrace before God His spiritual dealings, for He has completely delivered us and brought us into such abundance.

verse: ‘Cursed is he who dishonors his father or mother.’ And all the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
a: One of twelve curses answering to Israel's tribes, this strikes him who sets light by his father or mother. As in the ten commands, it follows the worship of God, honouring parents being next to glorifying God, the Father of all. The people's Amen owns that God's government curses what is contrary to His will, and only so are they morally qualified for His blessings.
b: A curse is pronounced on those who dishonor their parents, showing the importance of honoring one's father and mother as the next commandment after honoring God. This curse, along with others, demonstrates the seriousness of various sins that are sometimes hidden but will be revealed in eventual judgment, emphasizing the need for obedience to God's law in all aspects of life. The people's "Amen" signifies agreement with the righteous judgment pronounced. "For all on works of law, nothing but a curse awaits, emphasizing obedience to God’s law, highlighted by the people’s 'Amen' agreement with righteous judgment pronounced."

verse: “Then you shall be left few in number, whereas you were as numerous as the stars of heaven, because you did not obey the LORD your God.
a: Israel, once as the stars of heaven for multitude, promised to Abraham and fulfilled under Solomon, would be left a small, insignificant remnant. The divine curse would fall in full measure when disobedience hardened into disregard of the LORD's fearful name. The same covenant that pledged every kind of increase, where spiritual conditions were maintained, would bring diminishing upon a disobedient people.
b: The verse depicts how the Israelites would dwindle in number, contrasting their former abundance. The commentary highlights the severe decrease in population post-destruction, emphasizing their failure to obey God, leading to their diminished state. The stark contrast to the promise of a numerous offspring serves as a clear sign of God's judgment. Their vast numbers would dwindle drastically due to disobedience, a stark contrast to the promise of being as numerous as the stars, reflecting God's judgment on their failure to obey Him.

verse: “See, I have set before you today life and prosperity, and death and adversity;
a: Moses sums up the whole of his preaching of the law as life and good, death and evil. Life meant prosperity and salvation, death adversity and destruction, for the law, as the word of God, was living and powerful. In God's government life and good, death and evil are linked so that they cannot be separated. No man should dare to snap the link.
b: Moses outlines a stark choice for the Israelites between life and good, or death and evil, urging them to love the Lord wholeheartedly to secure blessings and avoid calamity. Obedience to God's law is key to their national life and prosperity in the promised land. Choose life that both thou and thy seed may live, for obedience to God is vital for national prosperity and blessings in the promised land.

verse: Had I not feared the provocation by the enemy, That their adversaries would misjudge, That they would say, “Our hand is triumphant, And the LORD has not done all this.”’
a: God abstained from utterly destroying His people only for His own name's sake. He would be provoked to wrath if the oppressors misunderstood Israel's ruin, boasting "Our hand is triumphant" and ascribing it to their own prowess. Men may think their hand is high, but God, using nations as His rod, will break it should they exceed their appointed limit.
b: God refrained from destroying His people completely, fearing that their enemies would boast of victory apart from His hand. The lack of understanding in Israel led to their deserving destruction, yet God's mercy restrained His wrath. The prideful boasting of their adversaries would falsely attribute triumph to themselves, denying God's hand in all they've experienced. Their enemies could falsely claim victory, disregarding God's hand, leading Him to restrain destruction to ultimately show His power and care for His people.

verse: he said to them, “Take to your heart all the words with which I am warning you today, which you shall command your sons to observe carefully, even all the words of this law.
a: Moses urged the people to take to heart all the words of the law, emphasizing the importance of observing God's commandments. They were to teach these words diligently to their children to ensure the continuity of faith for future generations. Jehovah's judgment on His people was influenced by their corruption more than external forces, highlighting the need for obedience in order to avoid destruction. In setting their hearts to God's law, the people were exhorted to ensure the faith's continuity for future generations and find true life and prolonged days in the promised land.
b: Moses once more impressed upon the people's hearts the importance of observing all God's commandments. This urging respects the whole law, not the song only, to be commanded to their children so religion might be perpetuated in their posterity. Moses' warning came from one who deeply felt what Israel would do against Jehovah in their stiff-necked folly and lack of thankfulness.

verse: So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
a: Joshua's fame spread throughout the land as the Lord was with him, fulfilling His promise to guide and prosper Joshua in all his endeavors. By following the counsel from the Lord, Joshua's wisdom, courage, and the miraculous victories achieved with God's presence made his name well-known in the country. Joshua's faithfulness, aligning with God's guidance, led to his fame spreading throughout the land as God worked miraculously through him.
b: The Lord was with Israel's leader, fulfilling His promise, counselling and directing him, and prospering him in all he engaged. His helper was the essential Word, Christ the Son of God, and his fame spread through all the land. Thus none who feared the Lord could from then on doubt that Israel's leader was the man appointed to succeed Moses.

verse: “Now behold, we are in your hands; do as it seems good and right in your sight to do to us.”
a: The Gibeonites, realizing the danger they were in due to the commandment of God to destroy all Canaanites, humbly submitted to Joshua's decision. In this surrender, they accepted any consequences with the hope of fairness and mercy, leaving it to Joshua's discretion to determine their fate based on kindness and justice. Humbly submitting to Joshua's discretion based on kindness and justice, "do as it seems good and right in your sight to do to us," the Gibeonites accepted any consequences with hope of fairness and mercy.
b: Fearing greatly for their lives, the Gibeonites placed themselves in the power and at the disposal of Israel's leader. Ready to submit, they left him to act with kindness and justice, particularly according to the league made and oath taken. Their safety lay in the name of Jehovah alone, though they remained cutters of wood and drawers of water.

verse: They did so, and brought these five kings out to him from the cave: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.
a: At their leader's command the cave is now opened by rolling away the stones, and the five kings are brought forth. They are named one by one, according to their dignity, for the greater glory of the conquest. Though these kings had combined against Gibeon, they must be broken, for Jehovah would completely put down the world's power before His people.
b: The Israelite warriors, in obedience to Joshua's command, unveiled the kings from the cave, including the rulers of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon. This symbolic act of complete subjugation was meant to inspire the Israelites for further engagements with the Canaanites, showcasing the victory over these kings and the glory of the conquest. The heavenly power shown in the victory over the five kings, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon, under Joshua's leadership highlights their complete subjugation.

verse: Thus Joshua took all that land: the hill country and all the Negev, all that land of Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, the hill country of Israel and its lowland
a: Joshua's conquest of the land of Canaan was comprehensive, covering from the southern Bald Mountain to the northern Baal-gad. He took diverse regions like the hills, Goshen, the valley, and the mountains of Israel, exemplifying God's favor during the victories. The detailed description signifies the continuous work of God in fulfilling His promises, reflecting the successful possession led by His divine power. Thus, Joshua conquered all territories as God commanded, ensuring the fulfillment of promises to Israel through unwavering obedience and divine intervention in their military victories.
b: Here follows a general view of the conquest. Goshen was pastoral land near Gibeon, while the lowland meant low places and campaign fields between the hills. The hill country of Israel denotes the mountainous part of Israel and Judah. Canaan was God's free gift to Israel, yet they had to fight for it, answering to the heavenly places.

verse: And Caleb said, “The one who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as a wife.”
a: Kiriath-sepher, also called Debir, must have been very strong and hard to conquer. Caleb offered his daughter Achsah as a prize to its conqueror. This drew out the latent energies of him destined to be Israel's first judge. Such an offer suited Caleb, in whom dwelt not simply faith but the energy of love that wholly followed Jehovah.
b: To spur bravery, Caleb promised his daughter Achsah to the conqueror of Kiriath-sepher, foreshadowing Othniel's role as a judge in Israel. This offer resembling Saul's gesture, represented marrying into the esteemed tribe of Judah. Caleb's offer of his daughter as a wife served as an incentive for bravery, a trait that defined Othniel's future role as a judge in Israel, reflecting respect and honor within the esteemed tribe of Judah.

verse: This was the inheritance of the tribe of the sons of Dan according to their families, these cities with their villages.
a: Dan's inheritance fell to the west of Benjamin, between Judah and Ephraim. It was formed as Judah gave up some northern towns and Ephraim some southern towns, furnishing the Danites a territory proportionate to their number. Dan's allotment came seventh in order, completing the division of Canaan among the twelve tribes by families, cities with their villages.
b: The tribe of Dan's inheritance included cities and villages, but they extended their territory to the north by conquering the town of Leshem. This tribe had land bordering Ephraim, Judah, Simeon, and the Mediterranean Sea, and it was distributed according to their families. Two saints harmoniously walk together, sharing the divine inheritance along borders with Ephraim, Judah, Simeon, and the Mediterranean Sea in brotherly grace.

verse: When the sons of Israel heard of it, the whole congregation of the sons of Israel gathered themselves at Shiloh to go up against them in war.
a: The congregation, in its heads and representatives, assembled at Shiloh intending to make war upon the two and a half tribes. This zeal was justifiable, even worthy of praise, for the altar might easily be abused and become an occasion of sin. Such an altar might stand in opposition to the tabernacle of Shiloh, setting up a rival centre of worship.
b: When the sons of Israel heard about the altar built by the two tribes and a half, they gathered together at Shiloh, ready for war, as they saw it as a violation of God's command for one sacrificial altar. Their zeal was justifiable, aiming to prevent potential sinful practices and preserve the unity of worship in the land. Their unity at Shiloh, prepared for conflict over the altar, stemmed from a commitment to God's intentions, exhibiting loyalty and discernment in their actions.

verse: And Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the sons of Reuben and to the sons of Gad and to the sons of Manasseh, “Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this unfaithful act against the LORD; now you have delivered the sons of Israel from the hand of the LORD.”
a: Phinehas, the son of Eleazar the priest, acknowledged the presence of the Lord among the tribes on the east of the Jordan, recognizing that God hindered them from committing a trespass, ultimately delivering the children of Israel from His judgment. This acknowledgment united the tribes and showcased God's gracious presence and protection. Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, preserving the tribes and uniting them through Phinehas' righteous intervention, demonstrating God's presence and protection among His people.
b: Speaking as the mouth of the group sent to them, Phinehas gives the glory to God alone, perceiving that Jehovah is among them. Because the eastern tribes had not committed this trespass, Israel was preserved from His judgments and the divine resentment. His pleasure lay not in the altar, whose omission might signal disapproval, but in their innocence, restoring national unity.

verse: Then Joshua dismissed the people, each to his inheritance.
a: Joshua let the people depart to their inheritances, each returning to his possession. This action marked the end of his leadership, with everyone going back to the lands assigned to their tribes. Joshua's final directive was to send each person to their allocated territory, marking the end of his leadership and the people's return to their own inheritances as assigned to their tribes.
b: The choice of Jehovah had been solemnly made, and the covenant renewed. Then Israel's leader let the people depart. Every man went unto, meaning to, his inheritance. He had done all in his power to establish them in fidelity to the Lord. Each inheritance was a heavenly inheritance, crowning God's ways of grace from Abraham's call until Canaan's full possession.

verse: So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He said, “Because this nation has transgressed My covenant which I commanded their fathers and has not listened to My voice,
a: The verse displays God's wrath toward Israel for violating His covenant through idolatry. Consequently, He chooses not to expel the Canaanite nations, leaving Israel surrounded by temptations and battles due to their defiance and failure to heed His instructions. God's judgment sends Israel into distress, turning them over to idolaters as a consequence of forsaking His covenant and not heeding His voice, ultimately inviting His disciplinary hand upon them.
b: The anger of the LORD burned fiercely against Israel because its idolatry was constantly repeated and grew worse and worse. They had transgressed the Sinai covenant forbidding other gods and had not listened to His commands. Yet the God who judges also has compassion, using their very lack of faithfulness to return them to the Word, their only safeguard.

verse: Deborah said to Barak, “Arise! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hands; behold, the LORD has gone out before you.” So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him.
a: Deborah's confident declaration to Barak marked the day the Lord would deliver Sisera into his hands. By asserting that the Lord had gone before them, Deborah filled Barak with courage as he led his ten thousand men down from Mount Tabor to face their enemies in battle. Deborah's act was right, but Barak's motive was wrong, and Deborah rebukes him severely, emphasizing the importance of a state in correspondence with the prophetic word.
b: Deborah's "Up" summoned Barak to rouse himself for battle, speaking of victory as given because of its certainty. Trusting that the Lord went before him, Barak relinquished the advantageous hill and rushed into the plain against the iron chariots. Ten thousand men were not much before Sisera's army, yet Jehovah went before them, making the victory altogether His praise.

verse: Gideon said, “All right, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, then I will thrash your bodies with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers.”
a: Answering the princes of Succoth, Gideon vowed to beat their flesh like grain with strong desert thorns. This cruel torture was often inflicted on captives in ancient times, thorns and briers being pressed upon naked bodies by sledges dragged over them.
