Gideon's threat awaits the Lord delivering Zebah and Zalmunna, for when the Lord comes He gives everybody what they deserve.
b: Gideon's severe warning to the princes of Succoth included a threat to punish them with thorns and briers if God granted him victory over Zebah and Zalmunna. This form of torture involved pressing thorns on their naked bodies, mirroring ancient practices used on captives. Gideon's severe threat mirrored ancient practices on captives, punishing the unhelpful with thorns on their naked bodies, revealing a lack of sympathy and self-importance in his approach.

verse: Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him; and many fell wounded up to the entrance of the gate.
a: Gaal proved far from a match for Abimelech, and a terrible rout began. He saved himself through the city gate, but the road to its very threshold was covered with the slain. His boasting had a miserable end. Abimelech was successful and the evil spirit triumphed, yet it became a scene of sorrow, slaughter, and hatred, not peace.
b: Gaal, unable to match Abimelech's might, fled as many fell "wounded, even unto the entering of the gate." Zebul, seizing the opportunity, banished Gaal who had earlier taken false pride in his leadership. Many fell wounded as Gaal fled before Abimelech, a warning of seeking self-prominence resulting in divine retribution, as revealed by the destructive path of Abimelech.

verse: Then the sons of Israel said, “Who is there among all the tribes of Israel who did not come up in the assembly to the LORD?” For they had taken a great oath concerning him who did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah, saying, “He shall surely be put to death.”
a: After a national assembly at Mizpah, an oath was taken that whoever didn't attend would face death, showing the seriousness of congregation meetings. When no one from Jabesh-Gilead was present, they were chosen to fulfill the punishment for not participating, despite the people's remorse for the outcome of their vow. The Israelites were determined to uphold their oath, even if it meant executing a severe vow against Jabesh to support Benjamin. The Israelites were resolute in fulfilling their severe vow against Jabesh, demonstrating the importance of maintaining righteousness with a divine savour, separating from evil while loving their brethren intensely.
b: The great oath, uttered when the national assembly was called, fell upon any who came not up to Jehovah at Mizpeh to consult about the Levite's concubine. Israel now determined to carry it out, seeking which tribe had not appeared. Their indignation bound them by solemn oath to drastic measures, yet with consciences outraged, they were not with God.

verse: Then she said, “I have found favor in your sight, my lord, for you have comforted me and indeed have spoken kindly to your maidservant, though I am not like one of your maidservants.”
a: Ruth, showing true humility, acknowledged Boaz's comforting words with gratitude and expressed her faith in finding favor in his sight. Despite feeling unworthy compared to his other servants, she appreciated the kindness and encouragement he showed her, bringing a sense of relief to her grieving heart. "Why have I found favor with you, who regard me, unworthy as a foreigner," is Ruth's humble response as she recognizes Boaz's personal kindness towards her, illustrating the Lord's personal favor towards his humble followers.
b: In true humility she wishes that Boaz might continue his kindness, for he had spoken to the heart of his maiden. Yet she deems herself unworthy to rank with the least of them, a poor Moabitish widow. His words sound like heavenly music to the poor stranger, yet his praise does not puff her up, for all is grace.

verse: She said, “These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said, ‘Do not go to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’”
a: Ruth excitedly told Naomi, "These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said, 'Do not go to your mother-in-law empty-handed.'" The six measures symbolized blessings or descendants to come; this act signified Boaz's kindness, hinting at positive outcomes, while also showing Ruth's sacrificial love for her family. Boaz's act of giving the six measures of barley hinted at spiritual blessings available, reflecting Christ's availability and the assembly's promise of inheritance.
b: She laid before Naomi six measures of barley, six seahs, rather a heavy load for a woman. Boaz's words, "go not empty unto thy mother in law," expressed compassionate concern for Naomi and gave assurance that she had well sped. Like the Holy Spirit of promise given as earnest, the barley was a pledge that Boaz would see the matter through.

verse: “May he also be to you a restorer of life and a sustainer of your old age; for your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him.”
a: The boy would be a restorer of Naomi's life and a refresher of the soul. He would also be one who would provide for her in her old age. Her daughter-in-law, who left family, home and gods for love of her, was better than seven sons. The child points ahead to the Messiah, a son born to afflicted Israel on a new ground of grace.
b: Ruth’s daughter-in-law Ruth surpassed the potential care of even seven sons, as her love for Naomi and the birth of a child brought restoration and support to Naomi's life and old age, providing her with joy and sustenance. Her love for Naomi made Ruth a restorer of life and sustainer of old age, symbolizing the saints' union with Christ and the intimate knowledge of Him as their Servant forever.

verse: The neighbor women gave him a name, saying, “A son has been born to Naomi!” So they named him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
a: The neighbours declared a son born to Naomi, for he was to her as a son. Obed means the serving one, alluding to his service of love and duty to his grandmother. From him sprung David and the Messiah. Naomi's case seemed hopeless, yet impossibility is a word never to be named with God.
b: The son born to Naomi was named Obed, which signifies 'serving.' This name highlights the service of love and duty he would render to his grandmother. Obed's significance goes beyond a mere title, as he is noted as the father of Jesse and ultimately the father of David. He who serves, Obed, was born to Naomi, reflecting the service and worship of saints who find redemption and blessings through their Messiah.

verse: -“There is no one holy like the LORD, Indeed, there is no one besides You, Nor is there any rock like our God.
a: As the holy and only One, the LORD stands in infinite superiority to everything earthly and human, with absolute completeness of life. He is the rock, fixed and immovable, in which the righteous can always trust. This praise of Jehovah's holiness contrasts sharply with Eli's sons' ungodly course and immoral dishonoring of His name.
b: The verse emphasizes that there is no one holy like the Lord, no one besides Him, and no rock like our God. The idea of holiness is tied to God's unique character as the one absolute God. The reference to God as a rock highlights His reliability and strength, especially in providing salvation. This comparison establishes God's unmatched nature and underscores His unmatched qualities and abilities. No one holy like the LORD, for there is none beside You, no rock like our God, highlighting God's uniqueness and strength, which believers reflect through holiness.

verse: So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. And as the ark of God came to Ekron the Ekronites cried out, saying, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel around to us, to kill us and our people.”
a: The ark of God was sent on to Ekron, the north-western city of the Philistines. Its inhabitants, thinking of the late occurrences, made complaint and protest against its entrance, fearing the God of Israel had come to slay them. The ark, God's testimony, could not be submitted to idols, and drew judgment on men thinking to prevail over God.
b: The Philistines sent the ark of God to Ekron, a city that had already witnessed the devastation the ark brought to Ashdod and Gath. The Ekronites were filled with fear and pleaded for the ark to be taken away, realizing the heavy hand of God upon them. The people of Ekron feared for their lives as they believed the arrival of the ark meant death and great calamity. "They have brought about the ark of the God of Israel to us, to slay us and our people," echoed the fearful Ekronites, realizing the divine wrath upon them, pointed out clearly by the earlier destruction in Ashdod and Gath.

verse: Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion that I gave you, concerning which I said to you, ‘Set it aside.’”
a: When Samuel instructed the cook to bring the meal he set aside, he meant the leg with attached fat, the best portion reservations for Saul as an honored guest. This act was to distinguish and honor Saul above the others, as Samuel foreknew his coming in a supernatural way. Samuel entertained Saul at the sacrificial meal by presenting this special portion kept for him. Samuel, obeying God's will, instructed the cook to bring the special portion for Saul, showing no jealousy but displaying dependence and confidence in communicating God's intentions to Saul.
b: Samuel told the cook to bring the portion, kept back in the kitchen till called for, the best piece. Its purpose seems to be to show Saul this was no chance-piece but one set aside for him, conferring honour and revealing Samuel's prophetic foresight. Saul was only a blind instrument in God's designs, while Samuel, confidant of His secret, had appointed this portion beforehand.

verse: The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Let us alone for seven days, that we may send messengers throughout the territory of Israel. Then, if there is no one to deliver us, we will come out to you.”
a: The elders of Jabesh requested a seven-day respite to seek help from all Israel. This was a display of their desperation due to the lack of a central government and dissatisfaction with the newly appointed King Saul. The messengers' journey to Gibeah of Saul indicated the recognition of Saul as the elected king, despite the need to appeal to the people, showing the transitional period from judges to monarchy. Recognizing Saul as king, the elders of Jabesh sought help from all Israel, illustrating a transition to monarchy and appealing to the people despite moral shortcomings in the narrative.
b: The elders, reflecting the universal form of civil government among the Israelites, asked seven days to seek a rescuer. Nahash had penetrated very far into Israelite territory. If no man came to save them, they would submit to be used at his pleasure. God could surely use a fleshly king as a rescuer, yet that work did not qualify him morally to lead Israel.

verse: Then Samuel said, “Bring me Agag, the king of the Amalekites.” And Agag came to him cheerfully. And Agag said, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.”
a: Samuel summoned Agag, the Amalekite king, who approached cheerfully, thinking his life would be spared. Agag, appearing delicately, expressed, "Surely the bitterness of death is past," hoping for mercy as he stood before Samuel, not anticipating his imminent demise. Approaching Samuel confidently, Agag hoped the bitterness of death had passed, but God's decree demanded his destruction against the pre-eminent enemy.
b: Samuel summoned Agag, the king of the Amalekites. Agag came delicately, or cheerfully, since he had gained the favor and protection of the king. Hoping his life would be spared, he confidently believed the bitterness of death was over. Yet from now on God's sentence against Amalek was confided to Samuel's hands, not to the disobedient Saul.

verse: “Let our lord now command your servants who are before you. Let them seek a man who is a skillful player on the harp; and it shall come about when the evil spirit from God is on you, that he shall play the harp with his hand, and you will be well.”
a: Saul's officers advised to find a skilled harp player to calm him when the evil spirit troubled him, showcasing music's medicinal effects on the mind and body. This music therapy foreshadowed David's future use of Psalms for comfort and peace. David's skillful harp playing, appointed for Saul's peace, mirrored his future use of Psalms to comfort and bring tranquility, showcasing divine intervention through music's soothing power.
b: Saul's court officers perceived the king's mental ailment and advised that the evil spirit troubling him be charmed away by instrumental music. This wicked spiritual power filled him with fear and anguish after the Spirit of Jehovah departed. After David's designation to the throne, Saul did not remain the same man, though Israel's destiny depended on his conduct.

verse: Again the Philistine said, “I defy the ranks of Israel this day; give me a man that we may fight together.”
a: Goliath's mockery lay in calling Israel the servants of Saul and in the triumphant tone of his challenge to single combat. He disdained them, as if not a man among them dared encounter him, and his challenge went unanswered. Yet he left God out, unaware that defying His people was defying God Himself, and here was his ruin.
b: Goliath's challenge to the Israelites was filled with scorn and contempt, as he called them slaves of Saul and boldly demanded a man to fight him. His defiance aimed to provoke the Israelite army, questioning their courage and daring them to engage in a decisive battle to settle the dispute. "I come to thee in the name of Jehovah of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied," declared David, as he stood fearless before Goliath, embodying the true representation of God in the face of the enemy.

verse: “And behold, I will send the lad, saying, ‘Go, find the arrows.’ If I specifically say to the lad, ‘Behold, the arrows are on this side of you, get them,’ then come; for there is safety for you and no harm, as the LORD lives.
a: Jonathan sets up a code with his servant to signal King Saul’s intentions toward David. Sending the lad to retrieve arrows, Jonathan’s instructions about the arrows guide David—“Behold, the arrows are from thee hitherwards, fetch them”—essentially indicating safety or danger based on the direction, assuring David's peace or flight. And if I expressly say unto the lad, 'Behold, the arrows are on this side of thee, take them; then come thou: for there is peace to thee, and no hurt; as Jehovah liveth, there is but a step between me and death.
b: Jonathan's sign lay in the lad sent to find his arrows. He might expressly say the arrows lay on this side of him. Then David might come, for peace was his and it was nothing, as truly as Jehovah lives. The lad himself would know nothing of the matter, which only Jonathan and David knew.

verse: But Jonathan answered Saul his father and said to him, “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?”
a: Jonathan answered his father Saul with the plea, "My father, why shall he die?" He asked what overt act of treason David had been guilty of, that he should be put to death. Through Jonathan's mouth David, a type of Christ, receives public testimony, yet Saul had not the smallest conscience toward God.
b: Jonathan, in an attempt to defend David's innocence and avoid his unjust death, questioned Saul, asking, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?" Saul's blind rage led him to hurl a javelin at Jonathan, revealing his unalterable resolve to kill David despite Jonathan's plea for reason and mercy. Jonathan was grieved for David, knowing David's rise would bring about the downfall of Saul's house, demonstrating faith in God's plan despite the imminent conflict.

verse: Samuel said, “Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has departed from you and has become your adversary?
a: Samuel's reply to Saul's query underscores the repercussions of straying from God's ways: "Why dost thou ask me, since the Lord has left thee and become thy enemy?" The shift of the kingdom from Saul to David signifies the grave outcome of seeking answers through forbidden means rather than following the Lord's lead. "Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has departed from you and has become your adversary?"
b: Samuel's answer exposes the contradiction in Saul's plea. The LORD had forsaken him and become his enemy. Then how could Saul expect an answer from Samuel, the prophet of Jehovah and His organ? Fear and superstition never reason. It is too late, for Saul now has both God and the Philistines against him, powerless and forsaken.

verse: They cut off his head and stripped off his weapons, and sent them throughout the land of the Philistines, to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people.
a: Saul's enemies cut off his head, placed it in the temple of Dagon, and sent messengers throughout the Philistine land to announce the victory. The sending of Saul's head and armor to their idol-temples served as signs of triumph, enhancing the Philistines' celebration of their idols' power and the victory they believed was granted by them. Their message of triumph and power was conveyed throughout Philistia by sending Saul's head and armor to idol-temples, glorifying the victory and exalting their gods.
b: The Philistines cut off Saul's head and plundered his weapons as trophies, sending them round about their land. These signs of victory announced the joyful news in their idol-temples and to the people, as though their idols' power had triumphed. A dead Saul did not feel the abuse but underwent it nonetheless, and the Philistines may have thought Goliath's death avenged.

verse: all the valiant men rose and walked all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.
a: The valiant men of Jabesh went all night to take the headless bodies from the wall of Beth-shan. Burning was not the custom in Israel, but was probably done so that the Philistines would not dishonor the bodies further. Jabesh-Gilead, once saved by Saul, showed pity upon the dead in a comely act, while all this ruin was dawn for David's reign.
b: The valiant men from Jabesh rose and worked through the night to retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons. Despite the unusual action of burning the bodies, it was likely done to prevent further desecration due to the gruesome state of the corpses, not to dishonor the anointed king. The valiant men from Jabesh rose through the night to protect Saul and his sons from further abuse, even though burning their bodies symbolized defeat by foreign idols and the king's fear of God's judgment.

verse: Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, “Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah? Today I show kindness to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers and to his friends, and have not delivered you into the hands of David; and yet today you charge me with a guilt concerning the woman.
a: Abner, furious at Ish-bosheth's accusation, responded with scorn, questioning why he was being treated like a despicable outsider when he had been loyal to Saul's family. Abner felt unjustly accused of wrongdoing regarding the woman and highlighted his loyalty in not handing Ish-bosheth over to David. Abner, likened to a dog's head, expressed frustration at Ish-bosheth's accusations, emphasizing his loyalty by not delivering him to David.
b: Abner, enraged at Ish-bosheth's complaint, asked whether he was a dog's head holding with Judah. He neither denied nor owned the fault with the woman, treating it as trifling beside his services to Saul's house. Yet his boast of withholding Ish-bosheth from David stands against how Judah, then all Israel, gradually recognize David's dominion.

verse: Meanwhile David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron; and more sons and daughters were born to David.
a: Alongside David's palace, David's house increased by the multiplication of wives and concubines, with sons and daughters born at Jerusalem besides those in Hebron. Yet he broke an express law forbidding Israel's king to multiply wives. The history of David as responsible king unfolds beside his history as Messiah's type, disobedient yet still dependent on God.
b: David, after moving from Hebron to Jerusalem, expanded his harem by taking more concubines and wives, contrary to the law. This multiplication of wives symbolized royal power. Despite his transgression, more sons and daughters were born to him, extending his lineage and royal legacy. Despite his transgression, David's increase in wives and sons fulfilled divine purposes, reflecting God's unique grace towards His chosen leader as he expanded his harem to symbolize royal power in Jerusalem.

verse: Then the king called Saul’s servant Ziba and said to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s grandson.
a: David summoned Ziba, who had been Saul's servant and perhaps steward. He announced to him the restoration of Saul's possessions to Mephibosheth. These were Saul's private estate at Gibeah. Hitherto a poor man, dependent on others, the grandson now received all his paternal estate. Though Saul's house had ever made war against David, its misery drew his grace, showing forth the kindness of God.
b: David called Saul's servant, Ziba, and declared, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s grandson." Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants, reflecting the responsibility he had in cultivating the land for Mephibosheth's provision. Though Mephibosheth dined at the king's table, he needed his own resources to care for his family and household. "Mephibosheth's portion cannot be taken away from him; he will 'eat bread at [the king's] table continually', bestowed the title of a son despite appearing wretched, embodying how misery attracts grace in David's act of kindness towards Saul's descendant."

verse: When all the kings, servants of Hadadezer, saw that they were defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and served them. So the Arameans feared to help the sons of Ammon anymore.
a: The kings, vassals of Hadarezer, saw they were smitten before Israel and became subject to them. This shows the great power of Hadarezer, and so Israel's strength under David. Hadarezer himself submitted, and Aram feared to aid the Ammonites further. Thus Ammon's allies, who sought to surround Israel's army, now served, while God held the reins as always.
b: When all the kings serving Hadarezer witnessed their defeat by Israel, they submitted to Israel and no longer supported the Ammonites. This highlights the power of Hadarezer and, by extension, Israel under David's reign. The complete victory over Hadarezer's servants led to them submitting to Israel, demonstrating David's power and authority during his reign, as Israel's enemies feared to support the Ammonites any longer.

verse: Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” And Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has taken away your sin; you shall not die.
a: David confessed to Nathan, saying, “I have sinned against the Lord,” exhibiting a genuine remorse that led to his acknowledgment of guilt without excuses. Nathan assured David of his forgiveness, declaring, “The Lord hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die,” signaling not a physical death but a spiritual one, demonstrating the Lord’s mercy and grace towards his repentant heart. Jehovah has put away thy sin; thou shalt not die, demonstrating divine mercy towards David despite the judgment for his immoral actions.
b: David's confession offered no excuse, no cloaking, no attempt to make his sin seem less serious. In response to this candid confession, the LORD let his sin pass by, forgiving it. David deserved death as a man who had committed adultery and as a murderer. Yet he would not die. Yet amid sorrow and discipline God had good things in store for the repentant king, who wrote Psalm 51 afterward.

verse: It came about after they had departed that they came up out of the well and went and told King David; and they said to David, “Arise and cross over the water quickly for thus Ahithophel has counseled against you.”
a: The priest's sons emerged from the well and urgently advised King David to cross the Jordan River quickly upon learning of Ahithophel's counsel. Responding promptly, David and his people crossed over by morning light, and the tide now turned in David's favor. Ahithophel's drastic choice to end his own life rather than face David's victory reflects his desperate attempt to escape the consequences of his failed counsel.
b: Once Absalom's servants were gone, the priests' sons came up out of the well and brought David the news. The water was the river Jordan. Ahithophel's counsel might yet prevail, so David must prepare against the worst. Jonathan and Ahimaaz formed one link in an uninterrupted chain of service, without which David would have become Absalom's prey.

verse: They took Absalom and cast him into a deep pit in the forest and erected over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each to his tent.
a: They took Absalom and cast him into a deep pit in the forest, covering him with a heap of stones as a dishonorable monument. This act, reminiscent of ancient traditions, marked the end of Absalom and his rebellion, causing all of Israel to disperse back to their homes, putting an end to the uprising. In the forest, Absalom faced his shameful demise under stones, illustrating the defeat of his rebellion as David's sorrow bespoke intertwined human tenderness and divine judgment in this heartbreaking chapter.
b: Absalom was cast into a great pit in the wood and covered with a very large heap of stones, a shameful monument like those raised over Achan. So ended Absalom and his rebellion, and all Israel fled home. Yet David grieved the irrevocable loss of the son whose salvation he had so deeply desired.

verse: -“Therefore the LORD has recompensed me according to my righteousness, According to my cleanness before His eyes.
a: The Lord recompenses individuals based on conduct, purity, and righteousness. Emphasizing divine response to human behavior and God's justice in evaluation, this verse underscores that purity and righteousness are key factors influencing divine rewards. The Lord responds to individuals according to their cleanness and righteousness, revealing Himself differently depending on their character, as evidenced by His connection with David as a prophetic symbol of Christ's perfection.
b: David declares the truth that God treats every man in accordance with his conduct towards Him. His recompense answers to his righteousness and to a cleanness seen before God's eyes, which the Psalm renders as "the cleanness of my hands." Yet David is celebrating the perfection of Someone other than himself, whose righteousness and cleanness Jehovah recompenses in His sight.

verse: -“Truly is not my house so with God? For He has made an everlasting covenant with me, Ordered in all things, and secured; For all my salvation and all my desire, Will He not indeed make it grow?
a: David's house stands in relation to God through an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, foreseeing even its bearers' falling away. It is preserved, for the Lord would not withdraw His grace, and David's salvation would spring up. Facing death, David condemns himself and his house, yet rests in a covenant God grounded in Himself, eternal and secure.
b: "Is not my house so with God that He has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and secured? For all my salvation and all my desire, will He not indeed cause it to grow? Although my house may not have flourished in uninterrupted worldly prosperity, God will faithfully maintain His covenant with my family until the arrival of the Messiah, who is the source of salvation and blessing." For this is all my salvation, and every desire, will He not indeed make it grow, springing up with a new people, relying firmly on God's promises and covenant with my family.

verse: Then Shimei arose and saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to Achish to look for his servants. And Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath.
a: Shimei disregarded the prohibition against leaving Jerusalem, hastening to retrieve his servants from Gath. His covetousness and lack of fear of punishment led him to act rashly, yet God's providence was at work, ensuring the servants were returned safely due to the peace between Gath and Israel. "He is judged by his own word: 'The word that I have heard is good.'"
b: Two slaves fled to king Achish at Gath. David had also found refuge there. As soon as Shimei knew, he started out and fetched them back. Achish, at peace with Israel and its tributary, did not detain them. Yet in leaving for Gath, Shimei took advantage of the goodness of God to bring a fresh slight upon Him.

verse: Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he also married Basemath the daughter of Solomon);
a: Ahimaaz from Naphtali possibly married Basemath, Solomon's daughter. His position did not encompass the southern region of Asher but rather stretched from the northern end of the lake of Gennesaret into Coele-Syria. This arrangement provided for a monthly provision and a matrimonial tie to the royal family. Ahimaaz, positioned in Naphtali, married Basemath, Solomon's daughter; his noble lineage tied to those who faithfully guarded the ark and connected him to Solomon's royal family.
b: Ahimaaz was possibly Zadok's son. He served as one of the king's chief tax-collectors in Naphtali. He gathered the produce of the land for a monthly provision to the royal kitchen. He also took Basmath, another daughter of Solomon, as his wife. This singular honor fell to one faithful to David at risk of his life, whom David called "a good man."

verse: Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;
a: Baanah the son of Hushai, likely a loyal companion of David, oversaw regions in Asher where abundant oil was produced. The reference to Bealoth could be a district or a place with ascending mountains, hinting at a location with steep terrain like the vicinity of the ladder of Tyre. Baanah the son of Hushai, who was likely a loyal companion of David, managed regions in Asher where there was plentiful oil; the mention of Bealoth might indicate a place with ascending mountains resembling the rugged terrain around the ladder of Tyre.
b: Baanah's father was probably Hushai, David's faithful friend and wise counsellor, and Baanah may have been promoted for his sake. As chief tax-collector he levied the king's duties in Asher, a very plentiful tribe, particularly for oil, and Bealoth. Baana was among Solomon's twelve stewards, a sign that all Israel was gathered under his scepter in one peaceful unity.

verse: He bought the hill Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver; and he built on the hill, and named the city which he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.
a: Omri purchased the hill Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, about 5200 thalers, and named the city after the former owner. Samaria, with its central location, became the capital where subsequent kings reigned, perpetuating a period of idolatry and disobedience, provoking the Lord's anger.
b: Once Omri had undisputed possession of the throne, he purchased the hill from Shemer for two talents of silver. He built upon it and named the town after the former owner of the hill. Samaria continued to be the capital of the kingdom of the ten tribes and the residence of all succeeding kings of Israel.

verse: The sons of Israel were mustered and were provisioned and went to meet them; and the sons of Israel camped before them like two little flocks of goats, but the Arameans filled the country.
a: The sons of Israel, mustered and provisioned, faced the Arameans as two little flocks of goats, playing the smaller force against the mighty Syrians. Despite their appearance, a prophet assured them of victory, leading to a remarkable triumph over the Syrian army by the omnipotent God of Israel. Assured by a prophet, Israel saw a remarkable triumph over Syrians, revealing God's touching patience and Ahab's humble response in defeat.
b: Mustered and provided for, Israel marched out and set up camp. They camped like two little separate flocks of goats, probably upon mountain slopes. They were few and weak yet compact. The Syrians, by contrast, filled the land with men, horses and chariots. The God whom Israel rejected reappeared as the God of deliverance, God of the valleys as much as the hills.

verse: Then one said, “Please be willing to go with your servants.” And he answered, “I shall go.”
a: The prophets sought to build a new dwelling, inviting Elisha to join them in choosing a place near the Jordan. With respect, one asked Elisha to come along, to provide guidance and protection. Elisha agreed, likely foreseeing the miraculous event that would transpire during their woodcutting expedition. "And he answered, 'I shall go,' foreseeing the miraculous events to transpire during their woodcutting expedition, as the sons of the prophets dwelled under the direction of the Spirit of Christ."
b: One of the prophets' pupils begged it as a favour that Elisha go with them. Awed by his presence, they might preserve peace and order. They might receive his advice on where to build. They might also be protected from men or wild beasts. Just like the Lord when Jairus appealed to Him, Elisha consents to come with his servants, answering simply, "I shall go."

verse: As he was relating to the king how he had restored to life the one who was dead, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life appealed to the king for her house and for her field. And Gehazi said, “My lord, O king, this is the woman and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life.”
a: Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life. At that very instant, the woman whose son was raised came and presented her petition to the king for her house and her land. Here again shines the character of grace of the prophet Elisha, testified even by Gehazi, the unfaithful servant now at the king's court.
b: As Gehazi recounted how Elisha restored the dead to life, the woman appeared before the king to request her property. Gehazi pointed her out as the beneficiary of Elisha's miraculous act, prompting the king to restore not only her house and field but also the land's produce. He recounted Elisha’s miraculous act faithfully, leading to the king's restoration of the woman's lost property, reflecting once more the grace evident in Elisha's character and pointing towards the return of blessings to Israel.

verse: The watchman reported, “He came even to them, and he did not return; and the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously.”
a: Coming nearer, the watchman could discern the manner of the company's driving. He saw it led forward madly. He associated this strange procedure with the known character of Jehu. Jehu drove without delay to Jezreel, where Joram lay sick. This furious driver was Jehu, whom one of the sons of the prophets had anointed in haste and secretly.
b: The watchman reported that the approaching troop was led forward madly, associating this behavior with Jehu's known character for driving furiously. Jehu's urgency in his driving was due to his active spirit and eagerness to seize Joram and ascend to the throne, fulfilling Elisha's prophecy regarding Naboth's blood being avenged in the field of Jezreel. He drove furiously towards Joram, fulfilling the avenging prophecy linked to Naboth's blood and showcasing God's judgment upon the house of Ahab through Jehu's urgent actions.

verse: Now the rest of the acts of Zechariah, behold they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
a: Zechariah's sins led to his public death by conspiracy, marking the kingdom of Israel's decline due to rejecting God's grace. All Zechariah's actions were carefully recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. All Zechariah's recorded actions in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel predicted the kingdom's decline and divine chastisement for adopting unscriptural practices, straying from God's ways in favor of following Jeroboam.
b: Zechariah's acts, be they more or fewer, good or bad, were recorded in the chronicles of Israel's kings. With his murder the house of Jehu fell, and the monarchy in Israel really ceased, his successors being mere robbers and tyrants. Such records belong to Kings, counted among the Prophets, a history whose prophetic authority the books of Chronicles confirm.

verse: He did evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done.
a: Jehoiakim reigned eleven years in the spirit of his ungodly forefathers. He was a bad prince who enriched himself by the unjust oppression of his people, with eyes and heart set "upon gain, and upon innocent blood to shed it." The Lord's warnings were lavished upon him by Jeremiah and other prophets, yet they were not heeded.
b: Jehoiakim continued the ungodly ways of his ancestors, focusing on personal gain even at the expense of oppressing his people. This led to a spiral of sin for the nation, eventually leading to its downfall, as seen in the reigns of Amon and Manasseh, all marked by evil in the eyes of the Lord. He did evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done, leading to the downfall of the nation, a fate foretold by Jeremiah due to idolatry and innocent blood, as history repeated itself from the time of Manasseh.

verse: To the sons of Gershom were given, from the family of the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan with its pasture lands and Ashtaroth with its pasture lands;
a: From the half-tribe of Manasseh, the sons of Gershom received the cities of Golan and Ashtaroth, which were provided with pasture lands. The plurality of names mentioned in the passage reveal details about the Levitical cities and the significance of the pasture lands as communal areas surrounding the cities for grazing. The list of priestly and Levitical cities was carefully structured with modernized or possibly new names added for clarity, highlighting the writer's attention to detail in recounting historical accounts accurately. The list meticulously structured with modernized names showcases historical accuracy, highlighting the connection between Judah and Joseph through the Levitical priesthood, hinting at the Messiah's kingly, first-born, and high priestly characteristics.
b: Gershom was one of the three sons of Levi, and his sons, the grandsons of Levi, are introduced. Here his descendants receive from the half-tribe of Manasseh Golan in Bashan and Ashtaroth, each with pasture lands. Golan in Bashan stands among the cities of refuge, listed after Hebron and Shechem in the same order as Joshua.

verse: and from the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead with its pasture lands, Mahanaim with its pasture lands,
a: From the tribe of Gad come Ramoth in Gilead and Mahanaim, designated as cities, with their surrounding pasture lands, the מִגְרָשִׁים, common grounds belonging to the cities. Noting that Ramoth in Gilead is a city of refuge, it's essential to recognize the missing mention in this account. In studying these passages, it's evident that there have been omissions and possible modernizations in the account. It is believed that the entire narrative has seen corruption, resulting in names and details being lost and needing restoration to complete the listing of cities. These three names - Judah, Joseph, and Levi - obscurely reveal the Messiah's kingly, first-born, and high priestly features, intertwined with Israel's genealogies and God's overarching purposes seen through David's lineage.
b: From the tribe of Gad the Levites, descendants of Merari, received Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge, and Mahanaim. In such cities not the Levites alone dwelt, but craftsmen and others from the other tribes. Ramoth in Gilead stands among the cities of refuge, for even such a list of names is not without profit for the soul.

verse: He said, “If the Arameans are too strong for me, then you shall help me; but if the sons of Ammon are too strong for you, then I will help you.
a: A promise of mutual aid is established between allies dealing with distinct adversaries. Joab strategically arranges himself against the Ammonites and entrusts another conflict to his brother Abshai. Political transitions are illustrated as the Moabites become tributary to David, indicating shifting alliances during this period. A covenant of assistance is made between allies, exemplifying mutual support in battle against different enemies, as seen when David pledges aid against the sons of Ammon if they overpower his ally.
b: These words belong to the detailed account of the Ammonite war, in which the Arameans and the sons of Ammon stood as foes. The speaker pledges help, should either the Arameans or the sons of Ammon prove too strong. Such military apparatus filling David's reign cannot be passed over in silence, for it belongs to the kingship established.

verse: the fifteenth for Bilgah, the sixteenth for Immer,
a: Bilgah and Immer received the fifteenth and sixteenth courses of the priests, assigned by lot. The lots of the two priestly families, Eleazar and Ithamar, were kept apart in different urns and seemingly drawn alternately. Immer's class is often mentioned. This ordering of priestly courses belongs to the history of David's family, the kings of Judah, not Israel's sovereigns.
b: The priestly classes were determined by the drawing of lots, ensuring fairness and equality in the distribution. The repetition of the same word signifies a distributive division, with each house representing two lots to maintain balance between the Eleazarites and Ithamarites. The fifteenth for Bilgah, the sixteenth for Immer, ensuring fairness in the distribution by lot among the priestly classes signifies balance and equality, spanning from the least to the chief fathers.

verse: the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his relatives, twelve;
a: Azarel is the Uzziel named among Heman's sons, the names varying like the king's names Uzziah and Azariah. All lots lay in one urn, and the eleventh place fell to him, with his sons and relatives twelve in all. Nothing was left to man's will, for the Lord decided each course of singers raising the temple's song of triumph.
b: Azarel was assigned the eleventh lot in the lineup of the musicians, alongside his sons and relatives. Each lot was drawn by chance, determining the order of succession amongst the sons of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman. The lots were all placed in one urn, with some names diverging in form as shown. The musicians, like the priests, were divided by God's free choice, showing that nothing was left to human will; the Lord's Anointed orders and the Lord decides, reflecting the importance of divine selection in these sacred duties.

verse: for the twenty-first to Hothir, his sons and his relatives, twelve;
a: The order of succession for the musicians was determined by lot, with specific sons of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman receiving designated places in a structured manner. The lots were not drawn individually for each chief musician but likely involved series of names included in the lot for selection. Divinely guided lots determined the musician's roles like the priestly courses, aligning precisely with God's ordained selection for each musician.
b: The twenty-first lot fell to Hothir, together with his sons and his relatives, twelve in all. His is one of the twenty-four names enumerated for these classes. Of these, only Mattithiah recurs in the bringing in of the ark. Such ordered service reflects kingship according to God's counsels in grace, completely fulfilled only when Christ is crowned.

verse: For the divisions of the gatekeepers there were of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.
a: The gatekeepers were arranged in divisions like the priests and musicians, drawn from families of the Kohathites and Merarites. Meshelemiah was a Korahite, and his ancestor Asaph was not Asaph the singer, a Gershonite, but the same as Eliasaph. Such ordering belongs to a book where the ways of grace make imperfect men capable of representing Christ's character.
b: The verse mentions the divisions of the gatekeepers, with Meshelemiah the son of Kore from the Korahites and Asaph's descendants involved. The gatekeepers were responsible for various duties, divided into classes like the priests and musicians, ensuring order at the sanctuary entrance. The gatekeepers' divisions reflect the priests and musicians' organization, requiring humility, zeal, and strength for their crucial sanctuary duties.

verse: then hear from heaven, from Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know Your name, and fear You as do Your people Israel, and that they may know that this house which I have built is called by Your name.
a: In Solomon's prayer, the conclusion appeals to God to hear the foreigners, wishing for all nations to revere Him like Israel does and acknowledge His presence in the temple. The request for God to arise to His rest signifies His presence among His people for salvation. In Solomon's prayer, the conclusion appeals for all nations to revere God, acknowledging His presence in the temple as Solomon, much more an intercessor than a king, prays for the people who may affect God's counsels.
b: Solomon's prayer begins with the joyful confession that the Lord had fulfilled His promise to David in the building of the temple. It then asks that all prayers made to the Lord in the temple be heard, even the foreigner's. Thus the blessing is not restricted to Israel alone, that the most distant nations might know and fear His name.

verse: The king answered them harshly, and King Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the elders.
a: King Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice, which led to severe outcomes. Despite fortifying the kingdom and appointing leaders, his humility prevented total ruin. In the end, God showed mercy due to Rehoboam's repentance and the presence of good things in Judah. His harsh response led to forsaking wise counsel, prompting the nation's transgression, but ultimately his repentance and Judah's goodness brought about God's merciful intervention.
b: King Rehoboam answered harshly and forsook the counsel of the elders, an event so important in its consequences. Behind it lay a decree of God, punishing the disobedience of the house of David through the revolt of the disloyal tribes. The division springs from Rehoboam's sin, not Solomon's, for he inherited not his father's wisdom but whatever was foolish.

verse: Abijah and his people defeated them with a great slaughter, so that 500,000 chosen men of Israel fell slain.
a: Abijah and his people inflicted a great blow on Israel, felling more than half of Jeroboam's whole army at Zemaraim. The number should not be taken strictly. Slain means strictly pierced, including both killed and wounded. This prodigious slaughter was God's righteous judgment on Jeroboam, destroying the men of war in which he prided himself.
b: Abijah and his people inflicted a decisive defeat on the Israelites, causing over 500,000 of Jeroboam's army to fall in battle. The word "slain" encompasses both killed and wounded, resulting in a significant victory for Abijah that surpassed the number of men he had in his own army. The realization of their complete lack of power brings Abijah something even more important than victory: they recover Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron — but especially Bethel, the place where the faithful God had given promises to Jacob.

verse: Moreover, they made an oath to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouting, with trumpets and with horns.
a: The people bound themselves by oath to the Lord with shouting, trumpets and cornets, to attest the sincerity of their return to Him. This oath was not extorted unwillingly but taken with the utmost cheerfulness and every demonstration of joy. Renewing the covenant after the revival brought on by the prophetic word, they rejoiced, having sought Jehovah with all their heart.
b: The people made a solemn oath to the Lord, vowing to punish any who turned away from Him, even to the extent of death as commanded in Deuteronomy. They proclaimed this oath loudly, with shouts of joy, and the sound of trumpets and horns, demonstrating their sincerity and happiness in renewing their covenant with the Lord. They made a solemn oath to the LORD, proclaiming it with shouts of joy, trumpets, and horns as a sincere demonstration of renewing their covenant with God, seeking Him wholeheartedly.

verse: “Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD and said, ‘I will entice him.’ And the LORD said to him, ‘How?’
a: A spirit deceived Ahab at the Lord's permission, showing God's sovereignty and protection regardless of textual variations. The narrative maintains a consistent theme of divine guidance, emphasizing the overarching power and influence of God throughout the events. "And this is all-instructive to us, that in going forth, the people of God went singing the song of victory, venturing and counting upon the Lord, reaping the fruits of faith in the valley of Berachah."
b: In the account of inquiring of prophets before the campaign against Ramoth-gilead, a spirit comes forward before the LORD, offering to entice the king. This narrative stands in almost verbal agreement with the record in 1 Kings. Though Ahab might hide from men's eyes, he does not escape God's eye or His judgment.

verse: “They have also emptied out the money which was found in the house of the LORD, and have delivered it into the hands of the supervisors and the workmen.”
a: The high priest, upon emptying out the money found in the house of the LORD, discovered the book of Moses' law. This significant find was promptly shared with state officials and ultimately read to the king. The money was delivered to those overseeing the temple restoration, as detailed to the king besides presenting the discovered book. Josiah's discovery of the Scriptures led to a deep confession, revealing the need for national repentance, symbolizing the rejection of idolatry, and paving the way for a feast of redemption to come.
b: Shaphan the state secretary tells the king about the money in the LORD's house. He says it has been emptied out and handed to the supervisors and workmen. This forms part of news passed from the high priest through Shaphan to the king. This money served to repair the house of Jehovah, begun in Josiah's eighteenth year after he had purged the land.

verse: “Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth and He has appointed me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah.
a: As the great kings of Persia usually did, Cyrus owns that he owes his power to a god, yet he expressly calls the God of heaven by His Israelitish name. He consciously entered into the purposes of the LORD, having probably learned of the God of the Jews and Isaiah's prophecies concerning him through Daniel.
b: Cyrus acknowledged the Lord God of heaven as the One who granted him his vast empire; upon taking Babylon, Cyrus recognized the prophecy of Isaiah, possibly through Daniel, as a directive to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. By attributing his success not to his own might but to divine providence, Cyrus demonstrated reverence for the God of the Jews and contributed to the fulfillment of God's plan through his decree for the temple's construction in Judah.

verse: the sons of Zaccai, 760;
a: The list in Ezra's account mixes town and personal names, emphasizing the priests' lineage and the return from Babylon as a symbol of Christ's future restoration and completeness as King and High Priest.
b: The sons of Zaccai, numbering 760, are reckoned here among the families who returned. The register counts the people both by family names and by places. Among the places are the men of Beth-azmaveth or of Kirjath-arim, Chephirah and Beeroth. Some families named in such lists reappear later among those who had taken strange wives.

verse: and of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael and 80 males with him;
a: The families listed in the passage were previously in Babylon and are now reuniting with their relatives in Jerusalem. These twelve families emphasize commitment irrespective of nationality, trusting in seeking God even amid opposition, showing humility and reliance on the Lord.
b: Zebadiah the son of Michael leads eighty males from the sons of Shephatiah, one of twelve lay houses named among these returning exiles. Like most of these races, the sons of Shephatiah bear a name already occurring in the list of those who came from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Their house was therefore already represented among the earlier returning exiles.

verse: All of them conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause a disturbance in it.
a: Learning that the wall's breaches were bandaged, the enemies were filled with wrath and conspired to fight against Jerusalem. Geshem incited the Arabians and Tobiah the Ammonites, while Sanballat the Horonite perhaps encouraged the Ashdodites to renew their old hatred of Judah. Acting in concert, they might suppose they could show the Persian king they acted on his behalf.
b: When the enemies heard that the walls of Jerusalem were being repaired, they conspired together to fight against it. The Jews prayed to God and took precautions, setting a watch and arming themselves. Despite ridicule, the people were determined to work, quickly repairing the wall. This verse shows the importance of trusting God, being courageous, and persevering in the face of opposition in order to complete the work set before us.

verse: I also applied myself to the work on this wall; we did not buy any land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.
a: Nehemiah dedicated himself to building the wall with his servants, avoiding any land transactions to maintain focus on the task. Their involvement showed Nehemiah's integrity and concern for the people's welfare, unlike previous governors who exploited them. By prioritizing the rebuilding rather than personal gain, Nehemiah led with a heart for the community's well-being.
b: The governor set his hand to the building of the wall, and his servants were gathered there for the work. Neither he nor his servants bought any land. They did not by the loan of money and corn acquire mortgages of land. Thus he shows the selflessness with which he filled his office for the good of his fellow-countrymen.

verse: the sons of Bigvai, 2,067;
a: The sons of Bigvai are named in the genealogical registry of those who came up at first from Babylon, with Zerubbabel and Joshua under Cyrus. This register was found while a resolution God had put into the heart was under consideration, to list the people's kinsmen as a basis for increasing the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The earlier copy of the list counts this family as 2,056.
b: Prompted by God, Nehemiah organized leaders to compile a list of their kinsmen from the genealogical registry of the first returning exiles, mirroring the list in Ezra 2, including the 2,067 sons of Bigvai, as counted in Ezra 2.

verse: For the Jews there was light and gladness and joy and honor.
a: The Jews of Susa, once facing the darkening of their future fate, now had light, a figurative expression for prosperity. With it came gladness, joy and honour, seen in the joy manifested by the city's inhabitants at the prevention of the threatened destruction. Their deliverance brought great and general joy where adversity had been.
b: The Jews in Susa experienced prosperity, joy, and honor due to the prevention of their threatened destruction. Their light and gladness represented their newfound prosperity and cheerfulness, while honor reflected the respect shown to them by others. This turn of events brought great joy not only to the Jews but to all of Susa, leading to a time of celebration and relief in the city.

verse: -“For He inflicts pain, and gives relief; He wounds, and His hands also heal.
a: Eliphaz's speech now becomes persuasive as he urges that God humbles in order to exalt. One and the same God woundeth and bindeth up, an image from binding up a wound when healing consisted much in external applications. His chastisement is therefore not to be received with a turbulent spirit. It is to be received resignedly, yea joyously. For the hand that bruiseth is the very hand that makes whole.
b: God, in His wisdom, sometimes allows afflictions to come our way, knowing that through the pain, He will bring healing and restoration. Just as a skilled surgeon sets a broken bone, God wounds but also binds up, showing His care and ultimate power to make whole. We can find comfort in knowing that even in the midst of suffering, God's hands are ready to bring about healing and redemption.

verse: Although there is no violence in my hands, And my prayer is pure.
a: The sufferer still claims that he does not deserve his sorrows. He insists there is no violence in his hands. He also insists that his prayer is pure. These calamities had not come upon him on account of any enormous sins, as his friends believed. His words are abrupt sob-like ejaculations, a requiem he chants for himself even while yet living.
b: Job insists his hands are free from wrongdoing and his prayers are pure. Despite his trials, he stands firm in his integrity, highlighting his adherence to righteousness and authentic worship. Job's appeal for fairness is underpinned by his conviction in his loyalty to God and his upright behavior in the face of adversity.

verse: Complete darkness is held in reserve for his treasures, And unfanned fire will devour him; It will consume the survivor in his tent.
a: Calamity awaits the treasures of the godless, with a fire kindled by God to consume him, even surviving remnants in his dwelling. All darkness is held in secret for the sinner, with judgment reserved among God's treasures, which will be brought forth in due time. This unkindled fire signifies divine punishment, extending to those left behind, illustrating God's judgment on the wicked.
b: Not wealth but all darkness, meaning every calamity, is hid for the treasures of the wicked. A fire not blown upon shall eat him up. It is the fire of God burning from within. It shall consume even the last remnant in his tent. Thus mercilessly does Zophar seek to stifle the new trust his suffering friend conceives towards God.

verse: -“How then will you vainly comfort me, For your answers remain full of falsehood?”
a: Job questions how his friends can offer him vain comfort based on false accusations. He highlights their lack of understanding of God's ways and the insincerity in their counsel. Job seeks genuine consolation rooted in truth about God's character and government, emphasizing that falsehood and error cannot bring lasting comfort. True comfort in trials comes from an unwavering belief in the righteousness of God's ways and a deep understanding of His purposes, enabling one to confidently endure suffering.
b: The sufferer calls his friends' boasted consolations vain, for facts contradict them. The wicked man escapes in the day of calamity and is buried with honor. Their answers therefore only betray evil intent against him. Instead of discerning his spiritual condition, they see in him only a constant wilful hardening against their urging to repent.

verse: -“Shall one who hates justice rule? And will you condemn the righteous mighty One,
a: Elihu asks whether it is even possible that an enemy of right should govern, since right and government are mutually conditioned. Without right everything would fall into anarchy and confusion. Applied to the Ruler of the world, the question becomes whether anyone would condemn the mighty just One, Him who is at once mighty and just, the All-just.
b: Shall one who hates justice rule? And will you condemn the righteous mighty One, even the All-just? Would it be conceivable that one who despises right and justice could govern or be fit to rule? Indeed, the argument stands that God, being the Just Ruler of the universe, cannot be unjust. Therefore, to condemn the One who is most just is to ignore His righteousness that governs all.

verse: “I know that You can do all things, And that no purpose of Yours can be thwarted.
a: Job, in his acknowledgment in Job 42:2, comes to a new realization of God's power as he reflects on the divine wonders of creation, exemplified by the behemoth and leviathan. As he contemplates the intricate plans of God, Job understands that even in the face of great suffering, God's purposes are beyond human grasp. Job's humbling realization leads him to admit his lack of understanding and accept God's wisdom in executing His righteous yet often incomprehensible plans.
b: Those strange but wondrous monsters prove to him that God can put everything into operation, and that His plans are beyond human comprehension. No longer murmuring or questioning, he frankly owns that Jehovah is able for all things. To his finite view God's purposes seemed bad. Yet they continue without anything stopping them. They will at last prove as good as they are wise.

verse: You destroy those who speak falsehood; The LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit.
a: The psalmist declares that God destroys those who speak falsehood and abhors those who are violent and deceitful. The wickedness of such individuals is detestable to God, whose holy nature cannot tolerate evil. This verse emphasizes God's righteous judgment against those who engage in deceit and bloodshed, illustrating His abhorrence towards wickedness and His commitment to justice.
b: God will destroy all those that speak lies. Jehovah hates the man of blood and deceit. This is the murderer who thirsts after blood and sheds innocent blood. The allusion is to the psalmist's enemies, who were false and treacherous. Wickedness and the wicked are here described in a sevenfold manner, though this is perhaps merely accidental.

verse: He lurks in a hiding place as a lion in his lair; He lurks to catch the afflicted; He catches the afflicted when he draws him into his net.
a: The wicked, lurking like a lion in its den, waits to ensnare the vulnerable and then swiftly captures them like a hunter seizing prey in a net. This imagery emphasizes the deceit and cruelty of those who harm the innocent, drawing them in with snares and allurements like a fowler trapping birds. The comparison to a lion and a hunter highlights the calculated and sinister nature of their actions, portraying a stark contrast between the victim and the one who preys upon them.
b: The wicked man, become as it were a beast of prey, lurks like a lion in his lair, a covered thicket. Then the figure is reversed, and the afflicted, the pious or meek sufferer, becomes the hunted beast. The wicked is a hunter who drives him into the pit-fall and drags him away in the net where he is entangled.

verse: How long shall I take counsel in my soul, Having sorrow in my heart all the day? How long will my enemy be exalted over me?
a: In Psalm 13:2, the psalmist's lament "How long..." encapsulates a soul wrestling with conflicting emotions, showing a mixture of despair and hope, hinting at a feeling of divine forsakenness. The constant sorrow and ineffective inner counsels portray an unrelenting battle against overwhelming odds. The enemy's prevailing signifies a bitter defeat and oppression, eliciting a plea for God's help in the face of relentless adversity.
b: The repeated cry of how long expresses a complicated condition of soul, in which, amid anguish under divine wrath, hope itself despairs, yet despair begins to hope. The counsels of his heart afford no relief, and his enemy is exalted over him. Yet faith holds fast the love behind the wrath, longing to see God's loving countenance unveiled again.

verse: He gives great deliverance to His king, And shows lovingkindness to His anointed, To David and his descendants forever.
a: God bestows great deliverance on His king, extending mercy to His anointed, David, and his descendants without end. This promise reaches beyond Israel, linking to the Messianic prophecy fulfilled in Christ, securing the eternal reign of David's line, and showcasing God's enduring favor towards His people. The continual protection and blessings given to David and his offspring resonate with divine commitments and the lasting nature of Christ's eternal kingdom.
b: God acts towards David as He promised, and the praise of His great deliverance shall not be confined within the narrow limits of Israel. These words echo the Messianic promises, whose fulfillment is found in the eternal reign of the Messiah. Praising the God of David, His anointed, is ultimately a praising of the Father of Jesus Christ.

verse: The earth is the LORD’S, and all it contains, The world, and those who dwell in it.
a: The earth belongs to the LORD. His throne of grace is set upon Zion. Yet His dominion is not limited like that of the heathen deities. His right to sovereignty embraces the earth and everything that fills it, everything found upon it and in it. Likewise the world, the habitable globe, and those who dwell in it, form a parallel expression, all belonging to Jehovah.
b: The verse emphasizes the vast ownership of the Lord over the entire earth and everything in it, including its inhabitants. As the Creator, God's dominion extends over every aspect of the world, from its natural resources to its people. Those who seek to draw near to God and live righteously are promised blessings and righteousness, marking them as His chosen ones. The psalm highlights the importance of living in purity and seeking the presence of God, especially for those who belong to His sacred family.

verse: For in the day of trouble He will conceal me in His tabernacle; In the secret place of His tent He will hide me; He will lift me up on a rock.
a: When trouble arises, finding refuge in God's sanctuary provides protection for David. This sacred haven signifies safety and a strong foundation beyond physical circumstances. David's longing for closeness with God shows his assurance of being securely hidden in the secret place of God's tent, shielded from foes, and lifted high on a rock.
b: David grounds his desire for God's house in what the sanctuary is to him. His tabernacle is a covered place of shelter where the Lord takes good care of those who take refuge there from the storms of trouble outside. There David is far removed from all dangers, lifted high above them, his feet upon rocky ground.

verse: The LORD will command His lovingkindness in the daytime; And His song will be with me in the night, A prayer to the God of my life.
a: In Psalm 42:8, the psalmist expresses his trust in God's continuous mercies, anticipating blessings even in dark times. He expects the Lord's favor in prosperity and in affliction, believing that even in the night of sorrow, God's comforting presence will inspire songs of praise. Prayer and gratitude to the God of his life resonate throughout this verse, affirming the psalmist's unwavering reliance on the ever-present, life-giving God, who remains his rock amid life's storms.
b: God Himself is indeed dishonoured in the psalmist, yet He will not suffer the trust reposed in Him to go unjustified. The psalmist relies on a constant flow of divine mercy by day, which will elicit his song by night. That song becomes a prayer to the God of his life, the prayer-filled sigh of yearning for deliverance.

verse: Be exalted above the heavens, O God; Let Your glory be above all the earth.
a: The psalmist's prayer rises to Him who dwells above and rules the universe. This hymn of praise shows how he links his own deliverance with God's glory. The cry to be exalted may mean that God be praised by the inhabitants of heaven and earth. Or it may mean that He show Himself in His exalted greatness over all the earth.
b: In this passage, the psalmist passionately calls for God's exaltation above the heavens and His glory to reign over all the earth. Through prayer, the psalmist expresses trust in God's ultimate supremacy and sovereignty, seeking refuge in His power amidst trials and enemies. The plea for God's honor illustrates a profound faith that God's intervention will not only bring deliverance but also magnify His name throughout the earth, reflecting the psalmist's unwavering confidence in God's unmatched authority.

verse: They have seen Your procession, O God, The procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary.
a: The verse describes the majestic procession of God as He enters the sanctuary, symbolizing His victory and authority over the world. The imagery portrays a triumphant God leading His people, as their King, to conquer challenges and celebrate His holy presence. This scene emphasizes God's power to subdue enemies and His role as the ultimate source of strength and salvation for His people.
b: Israel's festival of victory is pictured as a triumphal procession of God. He is the King who governs in holiness. He has subjugated and humbled the unholy world. All the world, especially the heathen who escaped the slaughter, have seen it. This deliverance is the counterpart of the deliverance out of Egypt, with the ark, symbol of His presence, leading.

verse: For my enemies have spoken against me; And those who watch for my life have consulted together,
a: The psalmist prays thus because he, who has been often amazingly delivered, is even now threatened by foes. His enemies speak against him. The watchers for his life consult together. They watch for an opportunity to take his life or destroy him. David himself had many such enemies, as Ahithophel and Shimei, who spoke against him.
b: Enemies claim God has abandoned me, leading them to conspire against me. When the wicked believe they have free rein because they think God has forsaken the innocent, they become more cruel and relentless in their persecution. The confidence of the evildoers in their ability to harm the righteous increases when they think God is not involved, but this should only strengthen the resolve of the faithful, for God's promises of help to the afflicted will surely be fulfilled.

verse: Why should the nations say, “Where is their God?” Let there be known among the nations in our sight, Vengeance for the blood of Your servants which has been shed.
a: The taunt of the nations, "Where is their God?", is a ground of pleading often used. This wish rests upon the words of Moses. The prayer is that God would step in so that none could doubt He avenged the blood of His servants. It is no cry of private passion but a plea for the whole Church.
b: The nations' inquiry, "Where is their God?" is a result of their guilt in mocking Him. The psalmist implores God for vengeance regarding the shed blood of His servants, hoping the nations will witness His justice openly. The sevenfold retribution depicts a thorough judicial process, affirming God's honor will not allow eternal triumph for the wicked. The longing for God's intervention is based on His pledge to avenge the blood of His devoted servants.

verse: Deal with them as with Midian, As with Sisera and Jabin at the torrent of Kishon,
a: The psalmist asks God to deal with these enemies as with Midian, recalling Gideon's victory, one of the most glorious recollections of Israel. He also recalls the triumph of Barak and Deborah over Sisera and the Canaanitish king Jabin, when the Kishon carried away the corpses of the slain army. He prays that God would prepare the same overthrow for Israel's foes.
b: Calling upon God to act against Israel's foes as in past victories (like Gideon's over the Midianites and Barak and Deborah's over Sisera and Jabin) ties these historical events at the Kishon River with divine intervention. The symbolic image of enemies becoming manure vividly illustrates their total defeat by the hand of God's chosen people.

verse: For it is He who delivers you from the snare of the trapper And from the deadly pestilence.
a: God's role is likened to that of a shield, saving believers from life-threatening snares, whether hidden or apparent. Like an eagle shielding its young under its wings, God ensures His protection is constant, guarding His people from harm, including the dangers of pestilence. The imagery used emphasizes God's unfailing defense against a range of perils, providing believers with confidence in His deliverance during times of trouble.
b: God delivers His people from the snare of the fowler. The snare is a figure for the peril of one's life. It means death or "he who has the power of death." In times of pestilence, the destroying angel can do no harm to him who has taken refuge in God. Snare and pestilence alike are expressive figures for various evils.

verse: Do not hide Your face from me in the day of my distress; Incline Your ear to me; In the day when I call answer me quickly.
a: The psalmist fervently pleads, "Hide not thy face from me in the day of my affliction," seeking God's attention during distress and asking for a quick response when calling upon Him. The urgency in the request stems from a deep need for God's presence and intervention, demonstrating the faith in immediate answers to prayer and the comfort it brings in times of trouble.
b: The psalmist opens with familiar expressions of prayer, words that rise in the heart and mouth of the praying one without feeling of foreign origin. He pleads that God not hide His face but incline His ear and answer quickly. Prayer may be answered at once, and the weak are invited to approach Him familiarly and confidently.

verse: And shed innocent blood, The blood of their sons and their daughters, Whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan; And the land was polluted with the blood.
a: Israel intermarried with the heathen they failed to extirpate. So they fell into a Canaanitish custom. In it the abominations of heathenism culminate: the human sacrifice of their own sons and daughters. This the Lord abhorreth, and only the demons delight in it. Thus the land was defiled by blood-guiltiness, and the people themselves became unclean by the whoredom of idolatry.
b: The Israelites sinned by failing to eradicate idolatrous practices and engaging in heinous acts of sacrifice, defiling the land with innocent blood, even that of their own children. This extreme cruelty and idolatry not only violated God's commands but also perverted the land He designated for worship. The stark contrast between Abraham's obedient sacrifice and this abhorrent behavior underscores the severity of the Israelites' transgressions.

verse: Many times He would deliver them; They, however, were rebellious in their counsel, And so sank down in their iniquity.
a: Here is sketched the alternation of apostasy, captivity, redemption, and relapse that followed the possession of Canaan, especially in the period of the judges. Failing to exterminate the idolatrous peoples, Israel shared in their idolatry, and the heathen became a snare to them. Though delivered many times, they rebelled and so were brought low in their iniquity.
b: Despite multiple deliverances, Israel persistently sinned by not obeying God's commands regarding idolatry in Canaan, leading to their own destruction. This cycle of rebellion, punishment, and redemption showcases both God's merciful nature and Israel's unrepentant behavior.

verse: The sea looked and fled; The Jordan turned back.
a: The dividing of the sea opens, and the dividing of the Jordan closes, Israel's journey through the desert to Canaan. The sea stood aside, and Jordan halted and was dammed up on the north so that the redeemed people might pass through. The psalmist sees the parted sea and the rushing Jordan arrested in its course, and asks in wonder what it means.
b: The Psalmist vividly describes the sea fleeing and the Jordan turning back at the mighty power of God, showcasing His control over nature in the exodus and entrance into Canaan. The image of the sea parting for the Israelites and the Jordan stopping to let them through symbolize God's divine intervention in their journey. The trembling mountains and hills further emphasize the awe-inspiring presence of the Lord, demonstrating His care and power over His people.

verse: Our soul has escaped as a bird out of the snare of the trapper; The snare is broken and we have escaped.
a: Our soul has been rescued by God, likened to a bird freed from a fowler's snare. Just as the bird escapes when the net breaks, we have been saved when the snare was shattered. This passage vividly portrays God's deliverance from the traps set by the enemy, allowing us to break free and find safety in Him who created heaven and earth.
b: In this joyful shout of the rescued one, the enemies appear as fowlers on account of their cunning. Israel's soul, threatened with great dangers, is a bird escaped out of the snare of him who lays snares. The snare was burst and Israel became free from what seemed, to all but faith, an overwhelming power bent on their destruction.

verse: Nor do those who pass by say, “The blessing of the LORD be upon you; We bless you in the name of the LORD.”
a: Passersby in the psalm are not blessing the workers in the field as customarily done, but rather, the enemies of Zion are likened to withered grass incapable of receiving such wishes of prosperity. The imagery serves to show the ineffectiveness of those who hate Zion and emphasizes that their efforts will not be successful in harming God's chosen people. It is a prayer that these enemies will not receive any divine or human blessing.
b: Israel's enemies are as grass upon the house-tops, never garnered in, so no passer-by offers them the harvest greeting. This greeting is taken from life and not denied even to heathen reapers, as Boaz greeted his reapers and was blessed in return. By contrast, before the righteous lies a garnering in of what they have sown amidst joyful greetings of blessing.

verse: To Him who spread out the earth above the waters, For His lovingkindness is everlasting;
a: The Psalmist's mention of God stretching out the earth above the waters showcases His wisdom and power in creation, reflecting His mercy in providing a habitable world (Jeremiah 5:22). This act not only established boundaries for the seas but also showcased God's care and intentionality in forming the earth (Genesis 1:1, 9). The imagery of the earth above the waters reveals God's benevolence in preserving life and preparing a suitable environment for humanity (Isaiah 42:5; 44:24).
b: The Psalmist praises God who spread out the earth, calling to mind the prophet's words of the Lord stretching forth the earth. It is said to lie "above the waters" because the water is partly visible and partly invisible beneath the earth. In that act God was preparing an abode for man, a lasting illustration of His kindness and enduring lovingkindness.

verse: To Him who divided the Red Sea asunder, For His lovingkindness is everlasting,
a: God's power and mercy are vividly displayed in Psalm 136:13 as it recounts the splitting of the Red Sea for the Israelites to pass through.
