Branches but externally and mechanically attached to Him bear no fruit, and the Father pulls them off and casts them away. Those vitally and spiritually connected He prunes, cleansing worthless parts and shortening rank growth, that their fruit may ripen and enlarge.
b: The Vine contains both fruitful and unfruitful branches, and the Father removes the unfruitful ones, while pruning and cleansing the fruitful ones. The disciples of Christ can either be spiritually fruitful or not, depending on their true connection to Him. The process of pruning and cleansing may be painful, but it is necessary and beneficial, allowing the fruitful branches to bear even more fruit. This emphasizes the importance of remaining spiritually connected to Christ and allowing Him to purify us so that we may bear fruit and serve Him more effectively.

verse: “He who hates Me hates My Father also.
a: In rejecting Christ, one also rejects the Father, as Christ is the sole embodiment of God to His creation. The weight of sin becomes evident in this rejection, brought about by the revelation that Christ's presence has provided. Dishonoring Christ is tantamount to dishonoring God Himself. Hatred towards Christ implies a corresponding hatred towards the Father, for the two are inseparable. However, followers of Christ can find solace and endure the world's animosity, as it serves as affirmation of their steadfast devotion to God.
b: Christ is the only manifestation of the Father to His creatures, so human regards of love or hatred towards Him are in fact directed towards the Father Himself. Such is the union between them that to dishonour Christ is to dishonour God. His coming has revealed the weight of sin on those who reject him.

verse: and stooping and looking in, he *saw the linen wrappings lying there; but he did not go in.
a: John, with reverence, chooses not to enter the sepulchre, instinctively noticing the undisturbed linen clothes. Peter, however, unafraid, enters the empty tomb driven by a sense of awe and mystery. It seems unlikely that the body would have been stripped naked, indicating that the linen clothes were not removed by a friend or enemy. John, with his timid nature, hesitates outside, stooping down to look inside but unable to gather the courage to go in alone.
b: Stooping to peep into the tomb, the disciple saw with simple sight the linen cloths lying there. He noticed this at once, for had the body been removed, these clothes would have gone also. Yet out of deep respect he held back from entering. It was not for fear of pollution. In all probability it was from a feeling of awe and mystery.

verse: and they were taking note of him as being the one who used to sit at the Beautiful Gate of the temple to beg alms, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
a: They recognized him as the beggar who sat daily asking for alms, and they were filled with awe and amazement at what had happened to him.
b: The people began to perceive that this was the very man who sat for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. He was the beggar they had seen asking daily. Recognizing him beyond doubt, they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. The once-familiar cripple at the gate had become an undeniable witness to the healing.

verse: And when they had summoned them, they commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
a: Having summoned them, they forbade them to speak or teach at all in, literally upon, the name of Jesus. They were not to make that Name the subject and basis of their speaking. The charge forbade them both to speak privately and to teach publicly.
b: The religious authorities ordered them not to make the name of Jesus the subject of their discourses, not to speak at all or teach in his name. The disciples were faced with a choice: to obey the authorities or to listen to God. But the message of Jesus was not something they could keep silent about. They understood that they were not only being told not to speak publicly, but also to withhold the doctrine of Jesus. However, they could not stay silent about the person, incarnation, offices, sufferings, death, and resurrection of Jesus.

verse: -‘THE KINGS OF THE EARTH TOOK THEIR STAND, AND THE RULERS WERE GATHERED TOGETHER AGAINST THE LORD AND AGAINST HIS CHRIST.’
a: In Acts, there is a conflict between those who stand with the Messiah and those who oppose him. The opposition to the Messiah is opposition to God himself. To despise and oppose the Messiah is to despise and oppose the one who appointed him. This conflict is not just temporal but holds greater significance. The true king, the Lord's Anointed, has replaced earthly rulers. Those who resist the gospel and set themselves against Christ are waging war against God.
b: Words of the second Psalm describe kings and rulers who set themselves in array against the Lord. They also set themselves against His Anointed, His Christ. The Jews understood these words of King Messiah. Opposition to the Messiah is opposition to God. Such enmity had appeared among the rulers of the Jewish people, and would grow as the gospel spread among nations.

verse: “For some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a group of about four hundred men joined up with him. But he was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing.
a: It is highly unlikely that St. Luke would have fabricated the words attributed to Gamaliel, especially considering the historical accuracy of Luke's other writings and his connection to St. Paul, who was a pupil of Gamaliel. Gamaliel's reference to impostors named Simon and Judas, who incited rebellion, adds credibility to his advice to let the apostles go. This cautionary tale serves as a reminder that those who advance themselves unadvisedly often face unfortunate consequences by the just judgment of God. While Gamaliel's mention of Theudas might have been historically contested, it serves to demonstrate that impostors and troublemakers often failed in their attempts. In the face of persecution and unmerited suffering, the apostles' unwavering dedication is truly commendable. Their steadfastness is all the more remarkable, considering the exemplary faith they exhibited after Gamaliel's advice of caution.
b: Gamaliel prudently mentions the facts first. He recalls Theudas, a man boasting himself to be somebody. Theudas led a revolt before that of Judas the Galilean. About four hundred men leaned to him, or took sides with him, giving credit to his pretensions. Yet he was slain, and as many as obeyed him were scattered and brought to nought.

verse: And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they kept right on teaching and preaching Jesus as the Christ.
a: Every day the apostles kept it up and ceased not to teach and preach the good news. They did this in the temple and in private, probably from house to house. Their going back to the temple was a distinct triumph. The substance of all their preaching was that Jesus the Crucified was no other than the Christ, the Messiah of promise.
b: Every day, undeterred by past punishment or fear for the future, the disciples proclaimed that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah. In private assemblies, they taught the doctrines of their Crucified and Risen Lord. Their constancy and joy accompanied their message, increasing their zeal for Christ amidst reproaches and persecutions. They declared Jesus to be the Son of God, the only Savior of sinners, who ascended to heaven and now intercedes for his people. Their example inspires us to continually proclaim Jesus, the hope of the world.

verse: “And behold, at that moment three men appeared at the house in which we were staying, having been sent to me from Caesarea.
a: Behold the remarkable coincidence as three men arrive at the house where the speaker is, immediately after his visionary experience. The visible presence of God's hand in this arrival cannot be ignored, as it carries an overpowering force that even the apostles and elders could not easily resist. The speaker emphasizes the significance of this arrival and highlights that he had received an express order from the Spirit to go with these men to Cornelius's house. Truly, this divine encounter was orchestrated by God's hand.
b: Peter is defending himself before the Jerusalem church. He had consorted with men uncircumcised. He calls his hearers, the people listening to him, to note the startling coincidence of this arrival. He says nothing of whose house it was, but names Caesarea and stresses that the men were sent to him. The apostles and elders were to mark the visible presence of God's hand.

verse: When they arrived at Jerusalem, they were received by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.
a: When Paul and Barnabas arrived in Jerusalem, the church, including the apostles and elders, warmly received them. This official reception was an expression of the church's hospitality and friendly acknowledgment of them as Christian brethren. During the gathering, Paul and Barnabas had the opportunity to share the remarkable conversion of the Gentiles and God's work among them. The church eagerly listened to their testimonies, recognizing the evidence of God's grace in their ministry and warmly welcoming them in affirmation and agreement.
b: On reaching Jerusalem, Paul and Barnabas seem to have been given an official reception in public by the whole church, including the apostles and elders. The word received implies a cordial welcome, which they were not altogether sure of receiving. There they gave a simple recital of how God had dealt with them among the Gentiles.

verse: After saying this he dismissed the assembly.
a: The city of Ephesus was known for its devotion to the goddess Diana, with thirteen other cities having a vested interest in the temple there. This reverence can be compared to the veneration of images and pictures in the Roman Catholic Church. Despite the tumultuous nature of the assembly, Luke's account of these events is seen as historically accurate. Gaius and Aristarchus, who were directly involved in these happenings, would have been witnesses to the vivid scene. By dismissing the assembly, Paul ensured the safety of himself and his companions, averting the imminent danger they faced.
b: With these words the town-clerk dismissed the irregular and tumultuous assemblage. He was keeper of the public archives and a magistrate of great authority. The assemblage had convened in a riotous manner. Luke's graphic picture has all the earmarks of historical accuracy. Paul was not in the theatre, but Luke evidently obtained the details from one who was there, perhaps Aristarchus.

verse: “And he said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will and to see the Righteous One and to hear an utterance from His mouth.
a: In his speech, Paul acknowledges the God of their fathers and the Just One, connecting their Jewish heritage with the Christian message. By mentioning the God of their fathers, Paul affirms the compatibility of the Christian doctrine with their faith in the one God of Israel. Ananias confirms that God has appointed Paul to know His will, see the Righteous One, and hear His voice. This divine appointment establishes Paul's authority and preparedness for service through his encounter with the risen Lord.
b: Speaking to Jews, Ananias names God and Christ by their Jewish titles, the God of our fathers and the Righteous One, a conciliatory touch. God's purpose for Paul is that he know His will, see the Righteous One, and hear the voice of His mouth. This places him on a level with the other apostles, who had seen the risen Lord.

verse: “But this I admit to you, that according to the Way which they call a sect I do serve the God of our fathers, believing everything that is in accordance with the Law and that is written in the Prophets;
a: Paul frankly confesses that he belongs to the Way, which his accusers call a sect in a bad sense. Yet he serves the God of his fathers, the ancestral God whom Roman law allowed every nation to worship. Believing all things in the Law and the Prophets, he claims Christianity as no deviation from Judaism but its fulfilment.
b: Paul defends himself against the accusation of being a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, boldly asserting his loyalty to Christ and the fulfillment of Judaism. Emphasizing his belief in the Old Testament Scriptures and the Messianic hope, Paul declares that his worship is not a deviation from true religion but a faithful continuation. By affirming his allegiance to the God of his ancestors, Paul counters the notion that Christianity is a schismatic sect, instead asserting its alignment with the teachings of the Law and the Prophets.

verse: Or do you think lightly of the riches of His kindness and tolerance and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?
a: The goodness of God, shown through His forbearance and long-suffering, is intended to lead sinners to repentance. This abundant goodness softens hearts and inspires gratitude, but contempt and ignorance frustrate its purpose. Sinners who become secure in their wrongdoing hinder God's desired course. Recognizing and responding to the true intention behind God's goodness is crucial, requiring a change of heart and attitude. Repentance, prompted by the kindness of God, is the necessary response to His abundant mercy and love.
b: The Jew who condemns others thinks down on God, despising the riches of His goodness, shewn by His forbearance and long-suffering. Forbearance is a holding back, a truce with the sinner that does not mean wrath will never come. His not knowing is a wilful and guilty ignorance, for God's goodness is designed and adapted to lead him to repentance.

verse: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.
a: The renewing of our mind is the instrument by which the metamorphosis takes place, as we discern and prove what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God. This transformation requires an inward spiritual transfiguration that makes our whole life new, unattainable without the constraining power of Christ's love. We are called to dedicate our whole being to Him, not conforming to the ways of this world but being fashioned by the renewing of our mind, living a life that is good, acceptable, and perfect in God's eyes.
b: Believers must not take this age as their fashion plate, the whole world of the ungodly. They are to be completely changed through the renewing of the mind. This is an inward spiritual transformation. It makes the whole life new in its motives and ends. So renewed, they prove by practical experience what God wills, that which is good, well-pleasing to Him, and perfect.

verse: For if because of food your brother is hurt, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.
a: To grieve a brother by our actions, especially over something as trivial as food, is an offense against love. By valuing our own desires above Christ's sacrifice, we risk destroying the souls of those for whom Christ died. Instead, let us live according to love, sacrificing our own comfort to promote the happiness of others. We should not cause our weak brethren to act against their conscience, leading them to eternal destruction. Love limits liberty and requires self-denial for the sake of others' spiritual well-being.
b: Food is purposely named as something worthless, setting the slight occasion against the great mischief done. Grieving a brother's weak conscience already breaks the rule of love, and may lead him to act against his conscience and be ruined. Since Christ died for even the weakest brother, value not thy, meaning your, meat more than Christ valued His life.

verse: But I have written very boldly to you on some points so as to remind you again, because of the grace that was given me from God,
a: Paul has written the more boldly only in some measure, perhaps referring to portions of the letter where he has spoken with especial plainness. Yet he writes not too boldly, but as putting them in mind. The ground and reason of his boldness is the grace given him of God, his office as Apostle of the Gentiles.
b: Paul writes more boldly to the Romans, confirming that his confidence stems from his apostolic office and the grace given to him by God. He specifically addresses passages where he has spoken with directness, acting as a humble reminder rather than assuming the role of a teacher. As an apostle of Jesus Christ, Paul emphasizes that his boldness is in line with his God-given duty to the Gentiles, reflecting the humility and authority of his office.

verse: For to us God revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.
a: God revealed the wonders of grace to believers through the Holy Spirit, solely by revelation and not by any native endowments of theirs. The Spirit searches all things, not in order to discover, but in ever active, accurate sounding of the depths of God. He knows God's nature, attributes and counsels, and teaches us those depths according to our capacity.
b: The Spirit of God, who is in us, searches the infinite depths of God and teaches us about His Essence, Attributes, and Counsels. While some may not comprehend the secrets of revelation, the Spirit reveals them to us according to our capacity. Without the Holy Spirit's revelation, doctrines remain lifeless outlines to the intellect, but the Spirit delights in revealing the depths of His divine mind to us. Through the Spirit, we have access to the deep things of God and can understand His profound plans and purposes.

verse: Now that no one is justified by the Law before God is evident; for, “THE RIGHTEOUS MAN SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.”
a: No man is justified by the law before God, whatever the case may be before men. He would not be justified even if he could keep the law. But he cannot keep it. Drawing on Habakkuk, Paul adds the scripture testimony, "The just shall live by faith." Life is promised and exists only in connection with faith, the condition of justification revealed in Scripture.
b: No one can be justified by the law, as even if someone could keep it, justification is by faith alone. The just shall live by faith, contrasting it with living by works. Justification by faith is God's chosen way, as no one except Jesus has fully kept the law. Therefore, we are not justified by the law but by faith, relying on Christ alone. This promise of life through faith is a continuous state of acceptance, life, and salvation.

verse: But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.
a: If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. The works of the flesh and the law are in the same category, while the Spirit and the law are opposites. Giving ourselves up to be led by the Spirit frees us from the works of the flesh and the bondage of the law. This freedom is granted by the Spirit, who emancipates us from the yoke of the law and leads us into the blessings and promises of the covenant of grace. The Spirit's guidance is for our profit and leads us out of sin and into the presence of God.
b: Paul sets the law and the flesh in the same category, saying not under the law where one might expect not under the flesh. Circumcision was a requirement of the law and a work of the flesh, and the law was weak through the flesh. Those led by the Spirit are under a different dispensation, the dispensation of the Spirit.

verse: SO THAT IT MAY BE WELL WITH YOU, AND THAT YOU MAY LIVE LONG ON THE EARTH.
a: It is surely a mistake to spiritualize this promise from the commandment, as though the earth meant the heavenly Canaan. The godly are equally blessed in every land, as the Jews were in the land God gave them. The promise is always fulfilled, either literally or by the substitution of a higher blessing, one spiritual and eternal.
b: Obedience to parents brings blessings, including the promise of a long life. The godly are blessed in various lands, and this promise is fulfilled either through a literal long life or a higher blessing that is spiritual and eternal. Disobedience to parents can result in negative consequences and God's judgments. The promise of a long life is to be understood both in a temporal and eternal sense. Obedient children who live long have an extended opportunity to sow seeds for the eternal harvest.

verse: having been buried with Him in baptism, in which you were also raised up with Him through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead.
a: Baptism is regarded as the burial of the former life, symbolically displayed through immersion. By being plunged under the water, believers declare their faith in the expiatory death of Christ for the forgiveness of past sins. Baptism serves as a picture of the change already wrought in the heart through faith, portraying the resurrection to new life in Christ. Emphasizing faith in God's energy as displayed in Christ's resurrection, baptism is a significant emblem of the believers' spiritual resurrection and the powerful operation of God in their souls.
b: In baptism the burial and the raising are both typified, picturing the resurrection to new life in Christ with an allusion to His own resurrection and to our final resurrection. Yet the new life is not caused by the act of baptism. It comes through faith, wrought in the soul by the same mighty power of God that raised Jesus literally from the dead.

verse: We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone.
a: These general instructions urging Christian duties seem addressed to the whole church, not to the church elders alone. The unruly, or disorderly, try the patience of leaders. The weak are those tempted to sin. Believers must lay fast hold on them so as to support them. Patience belongs toward all men, since no believer needs it not and none should be denied it.
b: In this instruction, the disorderly and spiritually weak are to be admonished and brought back into the right way. The feeble-minded, those affected by persecutions or loss, are to be comforted with the doctrines of grace. Moreover, the duty to support the weak in faith extends to all Christians, not just ministers. Patience is to be exercised towards all, and church leaders are called to strengthen, hold up, and bear the infirmities of fellow believers, fostering a unified and supportive Christian community.

verse: Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
a: This doxology is addressed to the Father as the King eternal, the King of the ages. He is immortal, or incorruptible, one who does not die, which distinguishes him from other sovereigns. The thought of eternity is terrible to unbelievers. But it is delightful to those assured of grace. To him belong honor and glory unto the ages of the ages.
b: To the King, the incorruptible and invisible God, be honor and glory for all eternity. God's reign extends over all ages and generations, distinguishing Him as the only eternal King. He alone possesses immortality and is the incorruptible God. Let us praise and admire His infinite wisdom, for He is the source of all grace. The thought of eternity is delightful to those who are assured of God's grace, as they find solace in the everlasting nature of His reign.

verse: not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another; and all the more as you see the day drawing near.
a: Gathering together as a congregation signifies the assembled body and should not be neglected. The day of Christ's second coming, which brings judgment, is always near. Assembling together fosters love, provokes good works, and strengthens unity. It is a sacred duty for believers to gather for public worship, as our graces are enriched in community. We should be diligent and encourage one another, especially as the day of Christ's return draws nearer. Neglecting the act of assembling may result in spiritual loss and potential apostasy.
b: Not forsaking means not leaving in the lurch. Our assembling together means the act of gathering. The same word is also used of the elect gathered to Christ at His coming. The habit of some pretty plainly shows not formal apostasies, but habits of negligence. Believers must encourage and urge one another in assembly, all the more as the Second Coming draws nearer.

verse: for our God is a consuming fire.
a: The little word for, meaning for also, introduces an additional solemn incentive to diligence. Our God, in whom we hope, is also to be feared, for He is a consuming fire. This is a most fearful image. It fits all that Scripture shows of His dealings with wicked people. It calls for reverence toward His holiness and justice.
b: For moreover our God is a consuming fire. The fact that God’s anger continues to burn against those who reject his Kingdom. The fire of God’s presence and purity becomes to His people, consuming their vanity, sin, and earthly state. Our God, whom we hope in, is also to be feared. He is love, yet there is another side of His character; God has wrath against sin. Thus, God omits nothing to draw us to Him, starting with love and kindness, but also using fear to bring about obedience.

verse: Grace be with you all.
a: The epistle closes with Paul's characteristic greeting, found in every one of his other thirteen Epistles and in no Epistle written by any other apostle in his lifetime. The grace meant is that of our Lord Jesus Christ. He does not express whose grace and favour he wishes for them, since that was a matter notorious to all Christians.
b: May the grace of God, specifically the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, be with all of you. This epistle is of utmost importance within the New Testament, and its absence would be noticeable. It serves as a key to understanding the Old Testament, and those seeking a thorough comprehension of the Bible should become acquainted with this letter. This verse echoes the customary benediction used by St. Paul, expressing the desire for God's grace to be upon the readers. May we personally experience the profound impact and application of this divine grace in our lives.

verse: And the seed whose fruit is righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
a: Righteousness is itself the fruit of the heavenly wisdom, now in germ, and shall be ultimately reaped. Its seed is sown in peace, as opposed to where envying and rivalry is, for only in peace is that fruit found. The ones who sow it are those who work peace, not merely they who reconcile others.
b: The peaceable fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by them who work peace. Those who are wise according to God's will make it their chief concern to sow righteousness, reproving sins with peaceable moderation. Only in peace is the fruit of righteousness found. The seed of righteousness is sown by the peacemakers in a spirit of peace. This righteousness promises a plentiful reward of happiness for those who make peace and labor to promote pure and holy peace.

verse: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though some strange thing were happening to you;
a: Beloved, do not be astonished at the passing through the fire which is taking place in your case for a trial to you. Think it not a thing alien from you but realize that some strange thing were happening unto you. It is not a strange and untoward chance, but rather it is taking place with the gracious design of trying you and proving you. Therefore, do not be amazed or consider it a strange thing. Instead, be prepared and steadfast, knowing that these fiery trials are permitted by the wisdom of God for your testing.
b: The fiery ordeal is like the fire by which metals are tested and their impurities removed. It is no strange and untoward chance, but a trial actually in progress, taking place with the gracious design of trying them. God has a wise design in it, a comforting thought for believers suffering in view of the approaching end.

verse: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
a: God is faithful to His promise and just in His dealing, and both attributes operate in the forgiveness of sins to those who repent. Confession of sin is urged throughout the New Testament, and pardon always supposes it. Forgive and cleanse together form one great complex act, to justify and to sanctify wholly and entirely, removing all unrighteousness offensive to Him who is righteous.
b: True confession of sin requires an external spoken acknowledgment and genuine inward contrition. God's faithfulness and justice are manifested in the forgiveness and cleansing of sins, leading to complete justification and sanctification. Confessing sin to God and to one another is a recurring theme in the New Testament. Forgiveness is not about justice, but about God's mercy, available to those who repent, believe, and sincerely confess. Through Christ's sacrifice, forgiveness of sin is immediate and comprehensive, while confessing with a penitent and believing heart guarantees God's faithful forgiveness and cleansing from all unrighteousness.

verse: The one who does not love does not know God, for God is love.
a: God is love. Love is the essence of God, co-essential with Him. He that does not love does not know God because God is love. Those who do not love never knew what love is for God is loving. God's love is not merely an attribute, but His very essence. Those who do not love have no acquaintance with God, never did get acquainted with Him. God is love; it is His darling, His reigning attribute that sheds an amiable glory on all His perfections.
b: God is fundamentally and essentially love, not merely loving. And so the one who does not love never knew love. Therefore he never knew God. Loving is the condition of knowing, for love is the expression of His personality corresponding to His nature. Yet the two terms are not interchangeable, since God is also light and spirit.

verse: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater; for the testimony of God is this, that He has testified concerning His Son.
a: We rightly accept the witness of veracious men, fallible though they be. Much more ought we to receive the infallible witness of God the Father. This is no particular testimony but a general one, even the fact that He hath borne testimony concerning His Son. So the Son comes, the Spirit witnesses, and the Father has witnessed.
b: If we accept the testimony of fallible men, we should surely believe the infallible testimony of God. The witness of God, including the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, is of greater authority and more reliable. Just as we accept the testimony of credible men, we should even more so accept the testimony of God. God is always true, and His testimony is the foundation of our faith in His Son. Through this testimony, we confidently believe that Jesus is the Son of God.

verse: Grace, mercy and peace will be with us, from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love.
a: Grace and mercy, given by God, address the guilt and misery of humanity. Peace, the blessed outcome, is obtained by casting all cares on the Lord. Truth and love are the essential conditions to receive and enjoy grace, mercy, and peace. The salutation reflects the wellspring of God's heart and His desire to relieve the afflicted. John emphasizes recognizing Jesus as the Son of God. This salutation encompasses the complete Divine blessing, rooted in truth and love.
b: The apostle includes himself in this greeting, a wish expressed by a confident assertion of its fulfilment. Grace has reference to men's sins and mercy to their misery, so grace comes first, and peace is the whole sum of both. These flow from the Father as their fountain and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, received in truth and love.

verse: Though I have many things to write to you, I do not want to do so with paper and ink; but I hope to come to you and speak face to face, so that your joy may be made full.
a: The apostle had many things to write, yet chose not to set them down with paper and ink, the Egyptian papyrus and ink made of soot and water. A heart full of love pours itself out more freely face to face, literally mouth to mouth. Their joy would be filled full in hearing from him in person the joyful Gospel truths he now deferred.
b: A heart full of love pours itself out more freely face to face, than by letter. Your joy will be complete in hearing from me in person the joyful Gospel truths which I now defer communicating till I see you. I would not write the many things I have to say now, but I trust to come to you and speak face to face, so that our joy may be full.

verse: Beloved, you are acting faithfully in whatever you accomplish for the brethren, and especially when they are strangers;
a: John praises the hospitality shown by Gaius, calling his care for the brethren an act becoming a faithful man. Whatsoever work or labor of love he performed for them showed that he had fully done his duty as a Christian. That the brethren he entertained were strangers only enhances the love manifested in the act.
b: In this commendation, the believer is praised for their faithful acts of labor and love, displaying genuine kindness towards brethren and strangers alike. Their sincere actions of generosity and hospitality are done out of a desire to glorify God and reflect their unwavering faith. The breadth of their compassion, reaching beyond their own community to include strangers, highlights their true spirit and integrity as a believer. Their selfless acts are not motivated by personal gain or recognition, but by a genuine love for others.

verse: Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.
a: Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. The one who does good is born of God, while the one who does evil has not truly experienced God. The word imitate in Greek carries the meaning of both an actor and a prose drama that portrays life and character. So, do not follow that which is evil, as seen in the actions of Diotrephes, but rather strive to imitate that which is good, which is exemplified in Demetrius.
b: John urges Gaius to imitate not evil but good, both spoken of in the abstract, probably with the contrast between Diotrephes and Demetrius in view. He that doeth good is from God, born of God and having his mission and power from Him. But he that doeth evil hath not seen God, spiritually, not literally.

verse: ‘But I have this against you, that you have left your first love.
a: The Lord has a somewhat against the Ephesian Church, one that threatens to grow to be an everything. Their early love, proof of the new life in Christ, had cooled off in spite of their doctrinal purity. Perhaps through controversies with the Nicolaitans, their warmth of love had given place to a lifeless orthodoxy, the letting go of the love of her engagement.
b: The Ephesian Church faces a reprimand for forsaking their first love for Christ and indulging in a stagnant orthodoxy. Despite their doctrinal purity, their love has grown cold, partly due to controversies with the Nicolaitans. This abandonment of their initial fervor is a serious matter, threatening to overshadow all commendable attributes. The Bridegroom longs for the intimate love of His bride, recognizing that genuine zeal must flow from a heart ablaze with affection. The Church's history vividly illustrates the perils of fervor devoid of genuine love.

verse: “And they overcame him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their life even when faced with death.
a: The faithful are constituted victors over the accuser in virtue of the shedding of the blood of the Lamb. They are also victors on account of the word of their testimony. They carried their not-love of their life even unto death, as Jesus himself had been "obedient unto death." Their victory marks the failure of Satan's endeavours.
b: They overcame by their faithful testimony, even unto death, showing their victory over Satan through the blood of the Lamb. Their holy lives, patient sufferings, and unwavering attachment to their Savior revealed the truth and power of religion, triumphing over their accuser. This victory, achieved by Christ's death, marks the failure of Satan's endeavors. The blood of Christ is the ground for their victory, and their love for Christ surpassed their love for their own lives.

verse: and he provides that no one will be able to buy or to sell, except the one who has the mark, either the name of the beast or the number of his name.
a: The calculated numerical value of letters in names point to commercial and spiritual restrictions imposed on non-conformity by both Pagan and Papal persecutors. Conformity and addiction to the beast's behests are symbolized by the mark, which may not be visible but rather allegorical. This mark resembles the sign of the cross in Popery, representing allegiance. The number of the name serves as a boycott against those who do not worship the emperor. The struggle of the Church against its enemies mirrors Christ's own struggle, facing degenerate Judaism within the Christian Church.
b: Here is a regular boycott, shutting out from buying or selling all who would not worship the beast. The mark may be, like the sealing of the saints, not a visible stigma but a sign of allegiance and conformity to the beast. It bears either his name or its number, the two being one, since letters carried numerical value.

verse: And another angel came out of the temple, crying out with a loud voice to Him who sat on the cloud, “Put in your sickle and reap, for the hour to reap has come, because the harvest of the earth is ripe.”
a: The Son receives the command from the angel to put forth His sickle and reap the harvest of the earth, as the time has come. This harvest signifies the gathering of the elect righteous, while the vintage represents the removal of the sinful. The command is not from the angel, but from God the Father to the Son. The temple is where God's judgments are proclaimed at their appointed seasons. The world is ripe for Christ's second coming, when the righteous will be gathered and the wicked will be dealt with accordingly.
b: Coming out of the temple, this angel does not command the Son of man but is the mere messenger of the will of God the Father. The Father keeps the times and the seasons, and sending the sickle recalls our Lord's own saying. The harvest, literally dried, is ripe, and the elect righteous are gathered as ripe for glory.

verse: When the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison,
a: When the thousand years are finished, Satan, no longer bound, shall be loosed out of his prison, the abyss into which he had been shut. The prophet speaks of this as still future. No hint is given why or how he is released, yet he is loosed in order that he may practise his work of deception on the nations.
b: When the thousand years are completed, Satan will be loosed out of his prison, signifying a future event where he will no longer be bound and will emerge from the abyss. This release of Satan will lead to a temporary outbreak of wickedness in certain parts of the world, although the reasons for it are unspecified. The saints will reign with Christ while Satan deceives the nations, resulting in joy in heaven, but woe on earth.
